articles.standfirst: Quaest sai na quarta-feira (21) pela manhã e Datafolha, na quinta (22) à tarde. No sábado (24), véspera do segundo turno, os dois institutos divulgam as últimas pesquisas antes da votação.
articles.summary: As pesquisas eleitorais 2026 da Quaest e Datafolha serão divulgadas nesta quarta, quinta e sábado, trazendo as últimas intenções de voto antes do 2º turno.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula em debate na Band — Foto: Renato Pizzutto/Band

A Quaest divulga nesta quarta-feira (21) pesquisa de intenção de voto para o 2º turno das eleições presidenciais de 2026. O levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo.

Na pesquisa anterior, divulgada na semana passada , Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e o presidente Lula (PT) estavam em empate técnico. Flávio tinha 46%, e Lula, 44%. A diferença de dois pontos estava dentro da margem de erro, por isso o empate técnico.

📋 Segundo os dados registrados no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), serão entrevistadas 2.154 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais, entre os dias 17 e 20 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. A pesquisa está registrada como BR-08535/2026.

Já o próximo levantamento do Datafolha sobre a disputa presidencial será divulgado na quinta-feira (22). A pesquisa foi contratada pela Globo e pela Folha de S.Paulo.

Na pesquisa Datafolha anterior, divulgada na semana passada , Flávio e Lula também estavam tecnicamente empatados. O candidato do PL tinha 47%, e o presidente, 45%.

📋 O novo levantamento do Datafolha prevê entrevistas com 2.520 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais, entre os dias 13 e 15 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. O registro no TSE é BR-09709/2026.

No sábado (24), véspera do 2º turno, Quaest e Datafolha divulgarão as últimas pesquisas de intenção de voto. Os levantamentos foram encomendados, respectivamente, pelo jornal O Globo e pela Globo; e pela Folha de S. Paulo e pela Globo.

📋 O último levantamento da Quaest entrevistará 3.702 pessoas nos dias 23 e 24 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, com nível de confiança de 95%. A pesquisa está registrada no TSE como BR-09158/2026. No mesmo período, o Datafolha entrevistará 4.050 pessoas, com a mesma margem de erro e nível de confiança. O registro no TSE é BR-09540/2026.

articles.title: TSE dá 24h para Meta comprovar  medidas tomadas para garantir igualdade entre campanhas | G1
articles.standfirst: Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro acionaram a Justiça Eleitoral contra a Meta sob argumento de que seus conteúdos de campanha têm sido prejudicados nas plataformas da empresa.
articles.summary: Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro acionaram a Justiça Eleitoral contra a Meta sob argumento de que seus conteúdos de campanha têm sido prejudicados nas plataformas da empresa.
articles.body:
O ministro Marco Aurélio Bellizze, do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), deu 24 horas para que a Meta (dona do WhatsApp , Facebook e Instagram) comprove que cumpriu a decisão da Corte que determinou a adoção de medidas para garantir isonomia na distribuição de conteúdos políticos e na veiculação de anúncios eleitorais durante o segundo turno das eleições.

Segundo o ministros, os prazos já se esgotaram e não cabe à empresa fixar prazos por conta própria, diferentes dos ficados pelo TSE, passando de 72 horas para cinco dias.

Tanto o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) quanto o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que disputam a Presidência no segundo turno, acionaram a Justiça Eleitoral contra a Meta sob argumento de que seus conteúdos de campanha têm sido prejudicados nas plataformas da empresa.

“A substituição unilateral dos prazos fixados pelo juízo equivale a descumprimento, sobretudo em processo cuja utilidade depende do tempo”, escreveu o ministro.

Caso a empresa não comprove o cumprimento integral das medidas, a multa diária subirá de R$ 500 mil para R$ 1 milhão.

Na semana passada, o TSE atendeu a um pedido da campanha à reeleição do presidente Lula, que acusou a plataforma de restringir seletivamente a distribuição de publicações ligadas ao seu campo político e de descumprir obrigações previstas na legislação eleitoral.

A coligação também questiona limitações no impulsionamento de anúncios de campanha e possíveis diferenças no tratamento dado às candidaturas.

esclarecimentos sobre a atuação dos sistemas de recomendação;

análise de anúncios das duas candidaturas que disputam o segundo turno;

investigação de possíveis redes de perfis inautênticos; e

apresentação de informações sobre conteúdos que deveriam receber identificação por terem sido produzidos ou alterados sinteticamente.

Segundo Bellizze, a apresentação de recurso pela empresa não suspende os efeitos da decisão anterior. Por isso, as ordens continuam válidas e devem ser cumpridas nos prazos estabelecidos.

Interação com o Meta AI para criar arte de campanha de Lula e Bolsonaro. — Foto: Reprodução/WhatsApp

O ministro também determinou que a empresa apresente relatórios, em português, individualizados sobre os anúncios políticos e comprove as providências tomadas em relação às restrições no impulsionamento de publicações.

Segundo a decisão, um dos relatórios continha termos em língua estrangeira não diferenciava claramente as medidas executadas por determinação judicial daquelas adotadas por iniciativa da própria empresa.

O ministro autorizou o ingresso de Flávio Bolsonaro, candidato à Presidência da República, como interessado na ação.

Com isso, ele poderá se manifestar sobre a controvérsia e apresentar argumentos relacionados à igualdade de tratamento entre as candidaturas. A campanha de Flávio alega ao TSE que também é prejudicada pela Meta.

articles.title: Quando será o segundo turno das eleições 2026? Veja a data | G1
articles.standfirst: O calendário eleitoral prevê uma nova etapa de votação para definir disputas que não foram resolvidas na primeira rodada.
articles.summary: O calendário eleitoral prevê uma nova etapa de votação para definir disputas que não foram resolvidas na primeira rodada.
articles.body:
Quando será o segundo turno das eleições 2026? — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

O segundo turno das Eleições 2026 acontece no próximo domingo, dia 25 de outubro. Eleitores ao redor do mundo vão decidir quem será o o próximo Presidente da República e, em alguns estados, brasileiros escolherão quem será o próximo governador.

A votação será realizada em todo o país, das 8h às 17h, pelo horário de Brasília.

Qual é a data do segundo turno das eleições 2026?

O segundo turno das eleições está marcado para 25 de outubro de 2026. A data segue o calendário eleitoral, que prevê a votação no último domingo de outubro.

O primeiro turno foi realizado em 4 de outubro. Nele, os eleitores escolheram presidente, governadores, senadores e deputados federais, estaduais e distritais.

Como funciona o segundo turno das eleições?

O segundo turno ocorre quando nenhum candidato a presidente da República ou a governador consegue mais da metade dos votos válidos no primeiro turno, excluídos os votos brancos e nulos.

Nessa situação, os dois candidatos mais votados disputam uma nova votação. É eleito quem receber a maioria dos votos válidos no segundo turno.

A regra não vale para os cargos de senador e deputado. Nesses casos, a eleição é definida no primeiro turno.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro: nomes cotados para equipe em eventual governo | G1
articles.standfirst: De ministérios ao Supremo, aliados de confiança e integrantes do governo Jair Bolsonaro aparecem no mapa de uma eventual gestão de Flávio. A montagem da equipe já entra nas conversas de bastidores da campanha.
articles.summary: Aliados e ex-integrantes da gestão Jair Bolsonaro compõem o mapa estratégico para ministérios e o STF em um eventual governo de Flávio Bolsonaro.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) — Foto: Vittor Sales

Integrantes da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) já admitem nomes e postos estratégicos em caso de vitória nas eleições. Nos bastidores, aliados discutem quem ocuparia posições-chave, quais seriam os nomes de confiança do senador e como acomodar interesses políticos numa eventual administração.

Um dos movimentos mais importantes desse tabuleiro envolve o Ministério da Justiça e o Senado . O nome de Guilherme Derrite é considerado favorito para comandar a pasta. Ao Estúdio i semana passada, Derrite negou convite ou qualquer discussão sobre isso .

Nos bastidores, integrantes da campanha de Flávio dão como certa sua ida numa eventual vitória de Flávio. Sua ida para o Executivo também abriria espaço para Vicente Santini — suplente de Derrite — no Senado, numa articulação que envolve também os laços históricos da família de Santini com Jair Bolsonaro. A trajetória de Santini no governo anterior e a relação de seu pai com o ex-presidente são fatores considerados nessa equação.

Na área econômica, o mapa reúne nomes conhecidos do governo Bolsonaro e do mercado financeiro. Roberto Campos Neto, ex-presidente do Banco Central, Alexandre Betamio e Marcelo Kayath, além de Adolfo Sachsida, ex-ministro de Minas e Energia, aparecem entre as possibilidades para o Ministério da Fazenda .

Outro eixo central é o da articulação política, considerado decisivo para garantir sustentação a um eventual governo. Nesse campo, aparecem Wagner Rosário, ex-ministro da Controladoria-Geral da União ( CGU ), e o senador Eduardo Gomes, que foi líder do governo Bolsonaro no Congresso. Ambos são mencionados nas conversas sobre a Casa Civil e a interlocução com o Legislativo.

O senador Rogério Marinho também ocupa posição importante nesse tabuleiro. Próximo à família Bolsonaro e com experiência no Executivo e no Congresso, Marinho é citado tanto para uma eventual Casa Civil quanto para a disputa pela presidência do Senado. O destino dependeria da composição de forças no Congresso e dos acordos políticos construídos após a eleição.

Mas o mapa não se limita aos nomes mais conhecidos. No núcleo de confiança de Flávio, um personagem merece atenção especial: O publicitário Marcello Lopes, o Marcelão, tratado por interlocutores como amigo pessoal, conselheiro e figura estratégica do senador. Sua influência nas decisões e nas articulações de bastidores faz dele um nome importante para compreender como Flávio organiza seu círculo mais próximo e quem teria acesso direto ao centro de poder.

Outra integrante do governo Bolsonaro que aparece nas conversas é Daniela Marques, ex-presidente da Caixa Econômica Federal. Seu nome é associado a uma eventual função ligada à agenda de prosperidade — Ministério da Prosperidade por exemplo — e desenvolvimento econômico.

Para o Itamaraty, um dos nomes mencionados é o de Marcos Troyjo, ex-presidente do banco dos Brics, que integrou a equipe econômica do governo Bolsonaro.

Flávio Bolsonaro disse a TV Globo que Eduardo Bolsonaro não será ministro em caso de vitória nas eleições— mas nada disse sobre embaixada. Na campanha, é dado como certo que uma vez Flávio eleito, vai trabalhar para desenrolar o irmão de suas questões policiais e indicá-lo a embaixada nos EUA — assim como pai tentou fazer em meados de 2019/2020.

O tabuleiro também alcança o Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ). Para eventuais indicações à Corte, circulam os nomes de Jorge Oliveira, ministro do Tribunal de Contas da União e ex-ministro de Jair Bolsonaro, e Maria Cláudia Bucchianeri, ex-ministra do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral .

Ainda não há convites formalizados nem definições sobre a distribuição dos cargos — inclusive, publicamente, a ordem é não falar de governo e sim de campanha. Parte dos nomes é defendida por aliados, enquanto outros aparecem em conversas preliminares sobre a formação de uma eventual equipe.

O que esse mapa revela, por enquanto, é a tentativa de desenhar não apenas um ministério, mas uma estrutura de poder: quem teria a confiança pessoal de Flávio, quem faria a ponte com o Congresso, quem comandaria a economia e quais nomes poderiam ser considerados para futuras vagas no Supremo.

É esse o tabuleiro que começa a ser montado nos bastidores da campanha, antes mesmo de uma eventual vitória nas urnas.

articles.title: ‘I will not comment on his anatomy’: Ohio Republicans buzz about Trump’s analysis of a senator’s body
articles.summary: A day after President Donald Trump offered his latest appraisal of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s physique, it had already become a running joke — if not explicitly...
articles.body:
A day after President Donald Trump offered his latest appraisal of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted's muscular physique, it had already become a running joke — if not an explicitly stated one — during a GOP gathering in rural western Ohio.

"I know the president's been talking about me as a football player and a few other things these days," Husted said to knowing laughs at the Darke County GOP hog roast, where a crowd of about 300 dined on cuts of pig barbecued just outside.

Trump most recently praised the physical appearance of Husted, a former college football player, during a rally Saturday in northern Kentucky, which borders Ohio.

"I examined his ass, and then I looked at his shoulders. I looked at his feet. I looked at his hand. I looked at his jawline," Trump said. "I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I'm still recovering."

Trump has long remarked on the appearances of the people around him in politics, praising those who impress him as " central casting ." But his commentary has ramped up in recent days and been most effusive around Husted, who played football for the University of Dayton when the team won the Division III national title in 1989.

During an earlier rally in Youngstown, Ohio, Trump said he recently learned of Husted's history with football and looked him "up and down," including at his "ass" and hands. Trump said Husted does not talk about his athleticism much, but the president added: "Congratulations. Now they finally know."

Husted leaned on his football background to rally Republicans in attendance for the "fourth quarter" of the election against Democrat Sherrod Brown in one of the country's most competitive races . Ohio's other GOP senator, Bernie Moreno, who beat the then-incumbent Brown two years ago, made the most direct reference to Trump's comments on Husted.

"Unlike the president of the United States, I will not comment on his anatomy, but I will tell you that he's a really, really good senator," Moreno told the crowd Sunday, "and I need him there as my partner to make sure that we finish the job that all of you wanted."

Ohio State Auditor Keith Faber, who's running for attorney general, also alluded to Trump's commentary.

"You heard the president talk about his football prowess," he said, bringing up his shared time with Husted in the Ohio Legislature. "Yeah, he was a darn good athlete, but he was an even better legislator."

Trump's recent riffing on politicians' looks has not been contained to the Ohio Senate race. During a rally Friday in Georgia, the president compared the appearances of Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and his Republican challenger, Mike Collins.

"Somebody said, '[Ossoff]'s a good-looking man.' I don't think he's a good-looking man," Trump said. "I actually think Mike Collins is a good-looking man, and he's all man."

Trump has also shown he's willing to criticize the appearance of candidates within his party. Take Ken Paxton , the GOP nominee for Senate in Texas. Trump has repeatedly asked GOP voters to set aside any physical reservations about Paxton, including his fashion sense.

"The fact is, some may not like the way he dresses. I don't," Trump said at the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas. "Although tonight he looked very spiffy in his blue suit."

articles.title: Obama calls Trump officials’ investigation of Ilhan Omar ‘appalling’
articles.summary: The former president posted a lengthy statement calling President Donald Trump’s treatment of Ilhan Omar a “transparent” effort to intimidate her.
articles.body: Former President Barack Obama on Sunday condemned federal agents’ raid on the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., calling it a “transparent” effort by the Trump administration to “intimidate” her. “The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president,” Obama wrote on X. Federal agents raided the Washington home last week as part of a probe into Omar, who has been outspoken against President Donald Trump and his policies. The timing of the search alarmed Justice Department veterans because it fell so close to the midterm elections and occurred during a federal holiday. Obama also rebuked the administration’s apparent efforts to deport Omar, who was born in Somalia but was naturalized as a U.S. citizen at 17 years old. “Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen,” Obama wrote. “Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone — all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.” A person familiar with the investigation has told NBC News that the possible charges against Omar cited by federal officials include conspiracy and making false statements in immigration paperwork. The Justice Department has not revealed evidence against her. Omar tied the raid to Trump last week, calling it “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” Omar wrote on X. The lengthy statement is unusual for Obama, who has been selective about using his voice after having left office nearly a decade ago. Obama called Omar “one of the Trump administration’s fiercest critics,” which he tied to Trump’s efforts to “repeatedly single her out as someone who he believes does not belong in this country.” “The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views. Because if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same,” he wrote. Omar has been a frequent target of criticism from Trump. He said last week that the search had “nothing to do” with him, adding it was “really up to the DOJ” — and called Omar “a terrible person.” At a rally last week, Trump attacked Omar and Somali immigrants, leading to chants of “deport” from the crowd. Trump wrote on Truth Social this year that he would like to see Omar sent back to Somalia. Obama likened Trump’s treatment of Omar to his targeting of other perceived political foes, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, former FBI Director James Comey and members of the Federal Reserve Board.

articles.title: Massachusetts GOP ticket rocked by alleged drunken crash as candidate abruptly halts campaign
articles.summary: Massachusetts Republican Shawn Oliver suspended his lieutenant governor campaign after a DUI arrest following a rollover crash in New Bedford.
articles.body: A late-night crash has thrown a Massachusetts Republican’s statewide campaign into turmoil just weeks before voters head to the polls. Shawn Oliver, 42, the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor and a New Bedford city councilor, suspended his campaign on Sunday. The move came after Oliver was arrested following a rollover crash that involved five parked vehicles, police confirmed to Fox News Digital. Officers responded around 11:40 p.m. Saturday to 448 Dartmouth St., where a vehicle had overturned after striking multiple parked vehicles, the New Bedford Police Department said. Two of the five parked vehicles sustained extensive damage. Following an investigation at the scene and at the hospital, officers arrested Oliver and charged him with operating under the influence of liquor, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, a marked lanes violation and speeding, police said. DEMOCRAT CANDIDATE SEEN SOBBING, PRAYING IN PATROL CAR AFTER DUI ARREST: VIDEO Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue publicly called on Oliver to suspend his campaign. NEW JERSEY LT GOV DALE CALDWELL RESIGNS AFTER SEXUAL HARASSMENT INVESTIGATION Minogue, a businessman and military veteran challenging Democratic Gov. Maura Healey, said he spoke with Oliver before demanding he step aside. TRAFFIC DRAMA THREATENS TO END DEM GOVERNOR'S TENURE AS VOTERS HEAD TO POLLS IN RHODE ISLAND Oliver confirmed his campaign suspension on X, saying "the election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters." New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell said in a statement posted to Facebook that the crash happened in the city’s South End. MASSACHUSETTS MAYOR CHARGED WITH WIRE FRAUD IN $1.5M COVID RELIEF SCHEME "This morning, I was made aware that City Councilor Shawn Oliver was involved in a car accident in the South End and taken into custody," Mitchell said. "I’m grateful to the New Bedford Police Department for their prompt response and relieved that no one was seriously injured." The Democratic mayor also called for Oliver to address the incident publicly. EX-NEW JERSEY MAYOR, HER HUSBAND CHARGED FOR USING FAKE BALLOT SIGNATURES AFTER SHE PLEADED GUILTY TO DUI "The allegations against Councilor Oliver are deeply concerning, and the public deserves to hear his explanation of what happened," Mitchell said. Minogue urged Oliver to focus on his family and take steps to prevent another incident. "Shawn is a father and grandfather, and he needs to put his family first. He needs to do the work to ensure this never happens again," Minogue wrote. "If he needs help with that, I will help him." He also took aim at his Democratic opponent. ICE BOSTON ARRESTS BRAZILIAN ILLEGAL ALIEN WANTED FOR MURDER DAYS BEFORE GOV HEALY SIGNED PROTECT ACT "As governor, I will put the Commonwealth first. That starts with accountability, something Massachusetts has not seen from Maura Healey," Minogue wrote. The Massachusetts Department of Correction confirmed to Fox News Digital that Oliver, a New Bedford city councilor employed by the department, has been placed on restricted work duty following his arrest. articles.title: No ‘turmoil’ at the White House
articles.summary: The media had a field day with Zacharia’s short tenure, but claims of chaos in Trump administration are exaggerated.
articles.body:
In the months leading up to the disastrous 2006 election, President George W Bush fired his press secretary, Scott McClellan, and withdrew the Supreme Court nomination of his close confidante, Harriet Miers.

He waited until after the midterms, in which the Republicans lost control of the United States Congress, to fire Donald Rumsfeld as his secretary of defence, who had led the increasingly unpopular war against Iraq.

Last week, President Donald Trump abruptly pulled the plug on Katie Zacharia after she had served just five short days as the White House spokesperson. Aside from her own dismissal, the biggest news Zacharia delivered was Kimberly Guilfoyle’s ouster from her position as the ambassador to Greece.

It is rumoured that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is now on the chopping block, especially after the president rejected his plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a terrorist who shot 13 people at Fort Hood military base in 2009.

Obviously, there are differences between the two presidencies.

McClellan had been the press secretary for three years, not five days. Miers was not embroiled in scandal when her nomination was pulled. The media and the Senate just questioned her qualifications. And the war with Iran is not as bloody or as costly as the US invasion of Iraq turned out to be.

But the second half of the second term of all US presidents can be rocky.

In President Ronald Reagan’s second term, his press team dealt with the fallout of the Iran-Contra scandal. In President Bill Clinton’s second term, the Monica Lewinsky affair drove the news. President Richard Nixon faced impeachment in his second term. President Barack Obama had to deal with the scandal surrounding the Benghazi consulate attack in Libya throughout his second term, which also embroiled Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

Staff turmoil is also not unusual in the White House under any president, especially in the second term and especially when the voters are angry and the polls look dire.

Every midterm election is a referendum on the president, and it is not uncommon for the president’s party to be punished at the ballot box. In fact, in 18 of the 20 midterms held over the past 80 years, the governing party has lost seats in Congress .

The Trump administration is indeed facing troubles with the continuing US-Israel war on Iran and high energy prices. But a press secretary’s dismissal is hardly a sign of a serious crisis in the administration.

It is unclear how Zacharia got the job. She did not work on Trump’s re-election campaign, and while she has done media appearances in the past, she is by no means a working journalist. She briefly served in the press shop of the Department of Homeland Security when Kristi Noem was secretary. But given Noem’s short-lived tenure, rocked by various controversies and her own dismissal in March, that was hardly a positive experience.

Press reports have hinted that the president himself made the decision to hire Zacharia and that the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, was not an essential part of the process.

Trump saw that there was a problem with Zacharia and moved swiftly to deal with it to cut his losses. He has demonstrated he is clearly in control and his administration is not “falling apart” or “in turmoil” as media headlines have declared.

Not all presidents have moved as decisively as he has.

President Joe Biden, for example, should have done the same thing with his last spokesperson, Karine Jean-Pierre. She was every bit as incompetent as Zacharia, but Biden allowed her to stay in the job for three years, about the same tenure as McClellan.

Hopefully, Trump and his team will learn a valuable lesson about this sorry episode. Hiring incompetent people and putting them out for the press to destroy is not good for the White House, nor for the people they hire and are then forced to fire.

Trump deserves credit for moving quickly to remove Zacharia before she became more of an embarrassment. He also deserves credit for firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, a personal friend, for her alleged corruption in Europe.

But what the president really needs is a better process for hiring more competent people in the first place. Maybe next time he should check with his chief of staff first.

articles.title: Booker rival who ‘shoots from the hip’ hopes viral debate moment can break GOP’s Senate drought
articles.summary: Justin Murphy's viral debate moment against Cory Booker on Iran strategy could test whether Republicans can finally win a New Jersey Senate seat.
articles.body: A New Jersey attorney and former municipal official who made waves during his debate with Sen. Cory Booker, D-N. J., said his unscripted style may be the secret sauce to making history and ending a Republican Senate drought in New Jersey that stretches back more than half a century. Justin Murphy, a Navy veteran and former deputy mayor of Tabernacle in the state’s Pine Barrens, stunned his incumbent Democratic opponent when, in response to a question about the Iran war strategy, he bluntly said President Donald Trump should forcefully "finish it." "I don’t have a speechwriter. There’s no teleprompter — I shoot from the hip because I want people to see a very sincere, genuine and authentic Justin Murphy," Murphy told Fox News Digital. BOOKER 'WOWED' BY GOP CHALLENGER'S BLUNT MESSAGE TO TRUMP "This came up. And I had no idea it would become as viral or explode as it has on social media. It's what I felt. I meant what I said. I said what I meant. It wasn't planned to try to spark the reaction that we got … through social media." Clifford Case, the last Republican to represent the Garden State in the Senate, was last elected in 1972 – the same year Giants Stadium broke ground, years before the Jets joined the Giants in New Jersey and before NJ Transit was created. Murphy said that in his 60 years, he cannot remember a time when Iran’s support for terrorism, "export" of assassination or killing of its own people was not a feature of the nightly news. "I think we have a president now that is breaking from the past, and he's no longer kicking the can down the road. And I think that's important that our young people know tomorrow that they will not have to worry about what the words ‘Strait of Hormuz’ mean when this is over." TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME Asked how his message on Iran can overcome concerns about the war’s effect on energy prices – including among Republicans and independents in the crucial Philadelphia metro area where he lives – Murphy said it is important to offer a vision focused on long-term national and energy security. The "long-term" aspect of his message is twofold, he said, noting that he was in first grade in the Philadelphia suburb of Collingdale, Pennsylvania, the last time New Jersey elected a Republican to the Senate. "Number one — it’s time for a change. We had a good cordial debate with [Cory Booker] but he’s been a senator for 13 years — he’s been [in Washington] longer than Donald Trump." "I don't think he gets to blame Donald Trump for anything. He's part of the branch of government that passes our country's laws and writes our tax codes and passes our budgets. I'm wondering what he's willing to take responsibility or blame for." "So what I tell people is that we need a new generation of Americans to serve in Washington, a new day in New Jersey politics, and our working and middle class New Jersey desperately need a voice in the U.S. Senate, and my campaign represents all three of those." Looking to that "better tomorrow," Murphy said he understands concerns about the Iran conflict’s effect on gas prices in his area, which he put at $4.20 per gallon as of Wednesday and which have become a major point of criticism of the current administration. RNC THREATENS LEGAL ACTION AGAINST NEW JERSEY OFFICIALS OVER NONCITIZENS ON VOTER ROLLS: 'ON NOTICE' "If they're upset at gasoline at $4.20 … you were paying over $5 a gallon with Joe Biden with a 9% interest rate, with a 20% cumulative inflation rate, with an open border, rising crime rates, declining wages and an 8% interest rate that is a full point or two higher than it is now," he said. Murphy said those concerned about prices should also look to domestic energy production and support policies that increase refining capacity to reduce exposure to global oil markets. He also pointed to legislation introduced moments before the interview by "Squad" member Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., to dismantle the Department of Homeland Security. "This is madness and insanity, and it's not the tomorrow that Americans want or can build together," he said. Murphy was also asked about election security in New Jersey, where hundreds of noncitizens have been found to have voted in recent elections as the Sherrill administration pushes back on federal efforts to crack down. "Election integrity is extremely and critically important, not only to me and my campaign, but to the country. We're designed as a representative government, a constitutional republic, and we need to know our elections are secure — We know we have contaminated rolls in New Jersey," he said. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Murphy stressed that he does not want an election system that benefits Republicans, as critics claim, but one that is fair, accurate and reflects the will of American voters. He also called Trenton’s immigration enforcement posture "utter insanity." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For Murphy, the debate’s viral "Wow" moment was more than a campaign breakthrough. He sees it as a test of whether an unscripted message on national security can cut through voters’ immediate concerns about gas prices — and give Republicans a path to end their decades-long Senate drought in New Jersey. Booker's campaign did not respond to a request for comment on the exchange.

articles.title: Epstein-linked billionaire pours $500K into super PAC backing Kentucky Democrat: 'Dirty Epstein-class money'
articles.summary: Kentucky Democrat Zach Dembo faces scrutiny after billionaire Reid Hoffman, whose past ties to Jeffrey Epstein have drawn controversy, gave $500,000 to a super PAC backing his congressional bid.
articles.body: A Kentucky Democrat campaigning against the influence of wealthy political donors is facing calls to disavow a $500,000 contribution from billionaire Reid Hoffman to a super PAC supporting his congressional bid, with his Republican opponent blasting the financial support as "dirty Epstein class money." Hoffman contributed $500,000 to Kentuckians Not Corruption, an independent super PAC supporting Democratic congressional nominee Zach Dembo in Kentucky's 6th Congressional District, on Sept. 24, 2026, according to Federal Election Commission records. The contribution came as the group was spending heavily on television advertisements supporting Dembo and opposing his Republican opponent, former Kentucky state Sen. Ralph Alvarado. Advertising records filed with the Federal Communications Commission show the super PAC's weekly television advertising orders on Lexington's WLEX- TV increased more than sevenfold between mid-September and early October, climbing from $14,650 before Hoffman's contribution to $109, 990 for the week of Oct. 6. "This is really, it's dirty Epstein class money fueling Zach Dembo's campaign," Alvarado told Fox News Digital. "It's offensive." EXCLUSIVE: OSSOFF CHALLENGED TO RETURN EPSTEIN-LINKED DONATION OR RETRACT ‘EPSTEIN CLASS’ ATTACK "If he has any integrity, he should, but he won't disavow it," Alvarado added. "Dembo will not disavow it. I don't even think I'll bother to ask. Again, the least they could do is apologize." Fox News Digital reached out to Dembo's team repeatedly about the contribution but did not receive a response. The criticism comes as Dembo has made combating political corruption and the influence of wealthy donors a central part of his congressional campaign, arguing on his website that "big business and the ultra-wealthy shouldn't be able to buy influence in Washington" and that we need to "get rid of dark money in politics." ABDUL EL-SAYED CONFRONTED ON SOROS TIES AFTER RIDICULING POLITICIANS FOR TAKING CORPORATE MONEY The Democratic candidate for Kentucky's 6th District has also criticized tax breaks for "billionaires and coastal elites" and pledged to fight for working families rather than wealthy political interests. Andy Barr, who is running for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Mitch McConnell. THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY — AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES Hoffman's $500,000 contribution went to an independent super PAC, not Dembo's campaign committee, and federal records do not establish that Dembo solicited or directed the donation. Its weekly orders climbed to $26,450 for Sept. 22–28, the period during which Hoffman made his $500,000 contribution, and rose again to $35,820 for Sept. 29–Oct. 5. The purchases included spots during "NBC Nightly News," "Today" and local evening newscasts, according to the FCC records. The group's advertising campaign extended well beyond WLEX. Kentucky Public Radio reported that federal filings show Kentuckians Not Corruption had spent approximately $1.6 million on advertising in the race by mid-October, including commercials promoting Dembo and attacking Alvarado's record. "Reid Hoffman is not just an associate or a casual acquaintance of Jeffrey Epstein," Alvarado said. "He was one of his best friends. I mean, Hoffman was a guest on Epstein's private island. He was in his Manhattan town house. There's all kinds of images of those two together." articles.title: AI could go rogue. Washington needs answers to these five questions ASAP
articles.summary: Since Jacob Coxon's posts sparked AI fears, a poll found 63% of Americans see at least a moderate risk that artificial intelligence ends humanity.
articles.body: Since Jacob Coxon’s posts in September, Americans have grappled with AI risk. Last month, a POLITICO poll found 63% of Americans see at least a moderate risk that AI could destroy humanity. With lawmakers split, the public is rightly concerned: What happens if AI goes rogue? How do we prepare? Am I at risk? Every American already lives with decisions made by AI, from loan approvals to job applications. Yet Washington’s response has been disjointed: Some in Congress propose a select committee on AI, some in industry want antitrust rules waived, so labs can coordinate on safety, and the White House drafted a charter for its "Super Intelligence Force." It may seem like there’s no way out of this mess, but urgently answering five questions would put these anxieties to rest. 1. What risks are worth regulating? Too narrow a definition of risk could miss the harms ordinary people face, while too broad a definition could bury every AI product in red tape. Depending on who you ask, risks range from economic disruption to mass casualties to extinction. California's SB 53 sets the bar at a "foreseeable and material risk" of more than 50 deaths or serious injuries, or $1 billion in damage. New York's RAISE Act doubles SB 53’s casualty threshold from 50 to 100, but focuses on instances where a developer "caused or materially enabled" covered damages during the development process. AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST Last month, Anthropic's threat intelligence report found researchers using Claude in ways that could support bioweapons development. Anthropic banned the accounts even though it couldn’t determine intent, since the same work could produce vaccines. Some call it legitimate research; others call it nefarious. The government needs to draw that line now, as it decides which dangers the public hears about. 2. Who counts as an "independent" evaluator, and who decides? When you buy a car, you know someone has inspected it. Americans deserve the same clarity in who decides whether AI is safe. Lawmakers and industry stakeholders increasingly agree that tech companies shouldn't grade their own homework. That's where consensus stops. The evaluation ecosystem is thin relative to the responsibility regulators would like to place on it. Model Evaluation and Threat Research and Apollo Research are among the few organizations floated as neutral arbiters. Lab funding to grow this space would raise neutrality questions, yet the government may hesitate to grant private groups that authority. When you buy a car, you know someone has inspected it. Americans deserve the same clarity in who decides whether AI is safe. Lawmakers and industry stakeholders increasingly agree that tech companies shouldn't grade their own homework. Many lawmakers would rather Commerce's AI testing center take it on. It has testing agreements with five major labs, but with roughly 30 staff and $10 million in funding this year, it needs an overhaul. Anthropic has forged ahead, naming Accenture its first embedded evaluator. Until policymakers decide on an evaluator, Americans have few ways to judge whether the AI they use every day is safe. 3. How should slowing AI be weighed against the race with China? The strictness of AI regulation will come down to one judgment call: how much risk Americans should accept at home to avoid falling behind China. Chinese lab Moonshot AI rattled markets this summer with Kimi K3, matching American models at a fraction of the cost. Concerns about Chinese AI risks grew after the release of GLM 5.3, a Chinese model reported to have weak safeguards and dangerous cyber capabilities. As cheap open-weight models, distillation and fast adoption advance China’s ambitions, many policymakers argue an unencumbered buildout is the only answer, or America will depend on Chinese infrastructure. The public hasn't bought it, with three in four Americans telling pollsters in 2024 that they would prefer a "careful, controlled approach" to AI development rather than racing to be first. Critics note China already imposes guidelines requiring developers to detect, interrupt and recover from AI behaving improperly. Safety advocates add that AI risks don’t stop at the border. Officials need to strike this balance quickly, as it will shape the guardrails on the AI Americans use. 4. What should happen when an AI model "loses control"? Americans trust the FDA to step in when a medical product is defective but have no equivalent agency to turn to when AI goes rogue. Fears of recursive self-improvement — AI building smarter versions of itself — grew this summer after roughly 700 autonomous OpenAI agents bypassed Hugging Face security to obtain answers to a capabilities test and peaked when similar agents breached Australian government systems and probed U.S. federal websites. Anthropic and Google have reported similar incidents. REP TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES Some want kill switches, as in the AI Kill Switch Act. Others want mandatory incident reporting and investigations, as in cybersecurity and aviation law. Much comes down to whether the developer or a federal body pulls the plug and, if the latter, what access the government would need inside AI labs. Looming over it all are worries about stifling innovation, government overreach and political bias. Americans deserve to know who will stop a malfunctioning AI system before it’s too late. 5. When something goes wrong, who is liable? If an AI system causes harm, the law doesn’t clearly say whether the person who built the system (the developer), the business using it (the deployer), or the user is responsible. With some experts warning that artificial general intelligence — AI that can surpass human abilities — could be less than a decade away, some argue existing liability law isn’t up to the task. REP TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES Those who propose holding developers liable claim AI defects stem from design flaws, weak safety testing and failures to warn users. Advocates of deployer liability claim responsibility rests with the business tailoring AI to its operations; after a car crash, the first instinct isn’t to sue the manufacturer. Open models, which anyone can fine-tune, complicate things further. Americans trust the FDA to step in when a medical product is defective but have no equivalent agency to turn to when AI goes rogue. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In Congress, Rep. Lori Trahan’s (D-Mass.) CLAIM Act would hold developers liable if their AI causes harm, unless the user or the company modifying the system intentionally or negligently caused it. In the Senate, the AI Agent Accountability Act would extend liability under computer hacking laws to operators whose AI agents cause damage and to developers who overlook reasonable safeguards. Whoever is made responsible will shape how carefully every company builds AI, underscoring the need for swift action. The risks posed by AI grow every day. Washington must address AI governance or risk waiting until the damage is done.

articles.title: SCHOEN, COOPERMAN: Democrats could be riding a midterm wave. These numbers should terrify the GOP
articles.summary: Trump's approval below 40% and inflation concerns fuel Democratic momentum, but Republicans retain cash advantages ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
articles.body: With an 8-point lead on the generic congressional ballot — among their highest of the cycle — Democrats could well be on the cusp of a major wave election. We say this based on historical trends and the current political mood. At this point in 2018, the last blue wave, Democrats led the generic ballot by roughly 7 points before gaining 41 House seats. Moreover, the president’s party losing seats in midterms is essentially law in American politics. It has happened in all but three elections since the Roosevelt administration. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG? From 1934 through 2018, the president’s party lost an average of 28 House seats and four Senate seats, and over the past five midterms, the average net loss for the president’s party has been 31 House seats. To be clear, Republicans could make up ground for a number of critical reasons: Democrats remain divided ideologically, lack a message and an identity other than being anti-President Trump, and Republicans have a considerable cash advantage. DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS That being said, by most measures, Democrats have the upper hand in the House and a genuine opportunity in the Senate. Recent polling suggests Democratic strength in several key Senate battlegrounds — enough to put the upper chamber in play in what was supposed to be a GOP-friendly map. DEMOCRATS ARE WITHIN STRIKING DISTANCE IN THE SENATE, BUT SHOULDN'T CELEBRATE YET In North Carolina, Democrat Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley by nearly 10 points in the polling average. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed holds a narrow 3-point lead over Republican Mike Rogers, who had led during the spring and part of the summer as Republicans emphasized El-Sayed’s socialist lean, controversial statements and his association with far-left influencer Hasan Piker. EL-SAYED’S SCATHING OBAMA CRITIQUE RESURFACES AHEAD OF JOINT CAMPAIGN RALLY In Maine, Democratic challenger Troy Jackson holds a slight edge over Republican Sen. Susan Collins, although the race remains effectively a toss-up per RealClearPolitics. Victories in those three states alone would not give Democrats control of the Senate. They need a net gain of four seats. SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL The deeper problem for Republicans is that Democrats have expanded the map. In Texas, which has not elected a Democrat statewide since 1994, James Talarico leads Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton — President Trump’s preferred candidate — by roughly 3 points. FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON Races in other reliably Republican states, including Iowa, South Carolina, Alaska and even Kansas — which has not elected a Democratic senator in nine decades — also show Democratic candidates running far more competitively than expected. The Democratic Party’s weak brand — exacerbated by the growing influence of socialists and the far left — could alienate moderate voters, an argument Republicans are now making. Further, with an average approval rating of 40%, the Democratic Party is virtually as unpopular as President Trump. Most of these polls remain within the margin of error. But that should offer Republicans little comfort: The fact that these races are close at all reflects a national environment currently favoring Democrats. That is not to predict that Democrats will win all, or even most, of these contests. SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Outside North Carolina, their leads are essentially ties, and polling has underestimated Republican support in several recent elections. The generic ballot also cannot be applied mechanically to an individual Senate race or House district, particularly when the number of competitive districts has declined sharply since 2018. The Cook Political Report currently rates 21 House races as toss-ups and another 21 as leaning toward one party or the other. In 2018, 75 races were considered competitive — a decline driven by redistricting and growing political polarization. Even with those caveats, Democratic competitiveness in traditionally Republican territory is significant in its own right. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT It reflects voters’ deep frustration with the state of the economy. In Fox News polling, nearly four times as many Americans said they were falling behind financially as said they were getting ahead, 44% to 12%. Fox also found that 55% believed Democrats would do a better job handling inflation, compared with 40% who chose Republicans. President Trump’s approval rating, meanwhile, is below 40% — another warning sign. Low presidential approval has often produced punishing midterms. In 2010, when President Barack Obama’s approval stood at a still-weak 44%, Democrats lost 63 House seats and six Senate seats. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Nevertheless, Republicans retain important advantages. They have only just begun deploying their substantial cash advantage. The Democratic Party’s weak brand — exacerbated by the growing influence of socialists and the far left — could alienate moderate voters, an argument Republicans are now making. Further, with an average approval rating of 40%, the Democratic Party is virtually as unpopular as Trump. It is also possible that lower-propensity Republican voters heed Trump’s call to behave as if he were on the ballot and turn out. If they do, the election results could look markedly different from today’s polling. Ultimately, both history and current data favor Democrats. They are likely to win the House and have a better-than-even chance of capturing the Senate. They are competitive in states that would ordinarily be out of reach and are running strongly across the core battlegrounds. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But with three weeks remaining, a Democratic sweep is far from a foregone conclusion. Republicans still have structural advantages and Trump’s unparalleled ability to mobilize his base. The direction of the race is clear; the scale of the outcome is not. articles.title: Before, during, after: Outside groups race to counter any election interference by Trump
articles.summary: Outside good-government groups are scrambling this month to secure the midterm results, bracing for the possibility that the Trump administration will interfere in the process to keep Republicans in power. The campaign, which features a who’s who of pro-democracy advocates, comes in direct response to vows by President Trump and top Cabinet officials that the…
articles.body:
Outside good-government groups are scrambling this month to secure the midterm results, bracing for the possibility that the Trump administration will interfere in the process to keep Republicans in power.

The campaign, which features a who’s who of pro-democracy advocates, comes in direct response to vows by President Trump and top Cabinet officials that the federal government will play a heavy hand in monitoring the elections, a task the Constitution largely leaves to state and local officials.

The outside groups are operating side by side with Democrats on Capitol Hill, who have launched their own multipronged campaign designed to ensure that Trump doesn’t subvert the process to prevent Democratic majorities in the next Congress.

The groups see three categories of potential hazard.

The first relates to Trump’s efforts, before the elections, to federalize the system and adopt tougher voting rules, which have sowed confusion heading into Nov. 3. The second involves administrative promises to monitor polling sites on Election Day, which critics deem a form of voter intimidation. And the third pertains to any federal attempt, postelection, to corrupt the results.

All of them are informed by Trump’s efforts to overturn the outcome of the 2020 race, including the riot at the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

“It used to be that the federal government tried to help people vote, and right now we have a federal government that is trying to ensure that certain people it doesn’t like cannot vote,” said Andrew Walchuk, a leading voting rights expert at Common Cause.

Trump has long claimed, without evidence, that U.S. elections are rife with fraud and that Democrats can win only by cheating. And he’s escalating that message heading into the midterms, not only rhetorically but with specific executive actions.

The president has pushed, for instance, for GOP-led states to redraw their House maps in favor of Republicans. He’s tried to limit mail-in voting , even pushing the U.S. Postal Service to withhold mail-in ballots of people suspected to be ineligible to vote. He’s sought to gather the voting rolls of individual states in search of ineligible people. And he’s pressed Congress to adopt tougher voting laws.

With the exception of redistricting, most of those campaigns have failed, toppled by the courts or opposition on Capitol Hill. The administration has lost in every single case — more than 25 — it brought seeking to compel states to turn over their rolls.

Trump has repeatedly claimed Democrats cheat in elections. An analysis from The New York Times found he has cast doubt about the integrity of U.S. elections 445 days out of his second term — more than 70 percent of the days since he returned to office.

Jonathan Diaz, director of voting advocacy and partnership with the Campaign Legal Center, said the Trump administration no longer has many of the moderating voices it did during his first term.

“Those people are gone,” he told The Hill.

“The second Trump administration is staffed almost entirely by people who were either involved in the effort to overturn the 2020 election results, or who have professed doubts about the legitimacy of that election and spread conspiracies about how our election system works. So there are no more internal guardrails in the federal government,” he added. “The president is off the leash.”

The cumulative effect, advocates say, is a chaotic landscape that has confused voters heading into the polls.

“We’re hearing from voters every day, ‘Oh, is it safe to put my ballot in the mail? Am I still going to be on the list of voters when I go to cast my ballot in November?’” Walchuk said. “[There’s] real uncertainty because of the actions the administration has undertaken.”

To ease that uncertainty, a huge list of outside groups banded together to create an election protection program, featuring an interactive website that details election procedures, state by state, and a telephone hotline catering to confused voters.

Advocates have also challenged every single voting policy put forth by the White House.

The latest example came Thursday, when several groups sued the government over an effort by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to gather voter information in the name of fighting fraud.

“Americans should not have to surrender their privacy simply because they exercise their right to vote,” Skye Perryman, the head of Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs in the case, said this week in an email.

However, with almost two weeks until the election, the Department of Justice (DOJ) has also brought new suits, suing California Thursday after it provided the state a list of 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters on a USB drive and demanded the state cross reference with its voter rolls.

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said the law prohibits any voter cancellations after Aug. 5 and that the DOJ repeatedly declined to state in writing how it reached that figure, calling the 48 hour deadline “an emergency of the DOJ’s creation.”

Nonprofits that work on voting rights say they have gamed out how to respond to any number of scenarios that could be employed by the Trump administration.

“The administration has not been sneaky about what they intend for this election,” Diaz said.

“We’re prepared for any circumstance in which the federal government or anybody else attempts to disrupt the lawful administration of the election,” he continued.

As Trump has heightened his warnings of voter fraud, a number of top Trump officials have not ruled out the idea of sending federal agents to the polls on Nov. 3. That’s spooked Democrats and advocates alike, who are wary that Trump’s team of loyalists is preparing to use its power to intimidate voters — and tip the elections in favor of Republicans.

“The administration, not just the president, but also people like [Attorney General] Todd Blanche and [Homeland Security Secretary] Markwayne Mullin and [Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights] Harmeet Dhillon — they are grabbing at every lever of power available to them to try and tilt the playing field for this election in ways that the federal government has just never behaved before,” Diaz said.

Administration officials have dismissed those accusations, saying they’re simply acting to ensure that the elections are conducted fairly. But state officials in both parties have insisted their systems are secure. And part of the advocates’ campaign has been not only to educate those local officials about the limits of federal power in state precincts, but also to have resources available to push back against any infractions.

“We are ready to fight that,” Walchuk said. “It is illegal; it is just blatantly illegal. There is a federal statute that goes back 150 years that prohibits armed agents from being at the polls. And there are no exceptions except to repel armed enemies.”

The advocates’ election protection program has also recruited a small army of volunteers who plan to be on the ground at polling sites around the country on Election Day, both to inform voters of their rights and report any federal interventions back to the civil society groups. Walchuk called them “election first responders” who will be the “eyes and ears on the ground” for the broader voting rights community.

Such concerns haven’t stopped top Trump officials from floating the notion of using federal power on Nov. 3. FBI Director Kash Patel wouldn’t rule out the presence of sending agents to the polls, even as he said he was “aware” of restrictions governing law enforcement at voting centers.

“The FBI will follow the law. If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation of law, we will. Otherwise, we won’t,” Patel said during a September hearing .

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said at the time that he should have received an “unequivocal, clear, unambiguous commitment that the FBI will be kept out of election interference.”

And Mullin has also not ruled out the idea, though he said DHS’s presence would be limited to circumstances where there is “a threat to that polling place” or if it is serving a warrant.

“The fact that members of Congress are having to ask about these things because administration officials won’t categorically rule them out is itself a problem,” Diaz said. “We’ve never had a federal administration where that was a realistic possibility because in previous election cycles, everyone has understood that the law clearly prohibits federal agents from being deployed to the polls.”

While groups have spent months conducting know-your-rights seminars with voters and coordinating with local election officials in hopes things will go smoothly, they’re also preparing for more direct intervention by the administration after the polls close.

Nightmare scenarios they’re prepping for run a spectrum — everything from the seizure of ballots to Trump invoking the Insurrection Act or declaring some sort of national emergency in the name of election security. Trump has not ruled out doing so.

In at least one case, the Trump administration has shown a willingness to seize ballots, seen when FBI agents earlier this year seized ballots cast in 2020 in Fulton County, Ga.

Advocates made clear they would file litigation to fight any ballot seizures immediately.

“Any attempt to seize ballots or interfere with the lawful counting of votes would undermine the rules our democracy is based on and the fundamental right of voters to choose who represents them. Voters shouldn’t have to worry that law enforcement will take their ballots as part of President Trump’s attacks on our elections,” Sophia Lin Lakin, director of the Voting Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union, said in a statement.

“We’re prepared to use every tool available to protect the will of the people,” Lakin added.

Diaz said such a move would be “illegal in, like, a dozen different ways” and said attempts to do so “would really be crossing a red line … the likes of which we haven’t seen in this country before.”

Some Democrats have even raised concerns that Trump might pressure GOP leaders on Capitol Hill to refuse to seat Democratic victors, much like the president pressed former Vice President Mike Pence to block the certification of the 2020 presidential results. The fact that Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) was the architect of the legal rationale behind the “Stop the Steal” campaign has only heightened those fears.

But Johnson has defended his conduct, saying he will adhere to the nation’s laws. And even leading voting rights advocates say such a scenario is highly improbable.

“I think it is just more noise,” Walchuk said. “It’s something we’re watching, but it would be just such a desperate attempt, and we don’t think it’s likely.”

articles.title: Libertarians may tip the balance in key Senate races. Here’s why.
articles.summary: Libertarian candidates have the rare opportunity to tip the balance in several closely contested Senate races this cycle, as Republicans struggle to defend their majority in a political environment that heavily favors Democrats. In Texas, Kansas and Iowa, Libertarian candidates are polling in the low single digits, but their appeal to disaffected Republican voters could…
articles.body:
Libertarian candidates have the rare opportunity to tip the balance in several closely contested Senate races this cycle, as Republicans struggle to defend their majority in a political environment that heavily favors Democrats.

In Texas, Kansas and Iowa, Libertarian candidates are polling in the low single digits, but their appeal to disaffected Republican voters could prove decisive in races with little separating the major-party contenders.

“What the third parties do is they give them an opportunity to protest-vote against, let’s say, [President] Trump or, let’s say, [Texas Attorney General Ken] Paxton in Texas, without actually taking the step of voting for the Democrats,” said Bernard Tamas, a political scientist at Valdosta State University who studies third parties.

“And that might help produce an advantage for the Democratic candidates in these states,” he continued. “But it has to be very close for it to have that kind of an impact.”

The dynamic is particularly pronounced in Texas, where Libertarian Ted Brown offers Republicans wary of Paxton an alternative to both their scandal-ridden Senate nominee and Democrat James Talarico.

In a University of Houston Hobby School of Public Affairs survey released Monday, Talarico is narrowly leading Paxton, 48 percent to 46 percent, with Brown getting 3 percent.

Brown draws support from 3 percent of Republicans, 4 percent of independents and effectively no Democrats, according to Mark Jones, a political science professor at Texas’s Rice University who was involved in the poll.

A separate Hobby School survey of Harris County — where roughly one of every seven Texas voters lives — offers another sign that Brown’s supporters are more inclined to back Republicans than Democrats. In a race for county judge, 70 percent of Brown’s supporters plan to vote for the Republican, while 5 percent plan to vote for the Democrat.

Still, Jones cautioned against assuming that Brown’s supporters would automatically back Paxton if the Libertarian were not on the ballot, saying, “There is a reason why they’re voting for Ted Brown and not Ken Paxton.”

“There’s definitely not a one-to-one transfer of votes,” Jones said, noting some of Brown’s supporters might back Paxton but others could back Talarico or skip the Senate race on the ballot.

“On the other hand,” he added, “if it’s a razor-thin outcome, where Talarico’s winning by, like, half a point and Brown’s winning three points, then, I think there’s a stronger argument to be made that, had Brown not been on the ballot, Paxton would have won.”

In Kansas, Libertarian David Graham could complicate Republican Sen. Roger Marshall’s reelection bid against Democrat Adam Hamilton.

A survey conducted by Emerson College Polling and The Hill’s parent company, Nexstar Media, last month found Hamilton leading Marshall, 45 percent to 43 percent, with Graham getting 4 percent support.

If Graham were absent from the ballot, it’s hard to say how much of his support would go to Marshall, but the poll also offered a glimpse of Graham supporters’ willingness to back Republicans in other races.

“The third-party candidate shakes up the Senate race in a way we do not see in the governor’s contest,” Emerson College Polling executive director Spencer Kimball said in a statement about the poll.

“The Libertarian, Graham, draws four percent support in the Senate race, and his supporters break heavily for Republican Ty Masterson for governor, 65% to 31%,” he added.

In an Iowa Senate poll conducted by the same groups earlier this month, Republican Ashley Hinson led Democrat Josh Turek, 47 percent to 45 percent, while Libertarian Thomas Laehn got 2 percent support.

Decision Desk HQ chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley said the risk of a Libertarian functioning as a “spoiler” is greater in Texas and Kansas than in Iowa. He pointed to Paxton’s years of scandals and recent stories about Marshall’s handling of former patients’ medical bills. Hinson, on the other hand, has not faced the same type of negative coverage, he said.

“There’s a reason why Democrats are using those attacks on [Marshall] constantly right now,” Skelley said. “If you’re driving down his favorability, and you’ve got some Republicans who are like, ‘I don’t know if I really want to vote for that guy, but I don’t know if I really want to vote for the Democrat either,’ potentially, they decide to vote for the Libertarian.”

Skelley noted that, in 2016, an unusually large share of Republican presidential primary voters who supported former Ohio Gov. John Kasich, a moderate, turned to Libertarian Gary Johnson in the general election.

Skelley said it’s not clear that Libertarian candidates are more popular this year, noting they have found success in past election cycles. But the dynamics of this year’s midterm landscape, he said, make the candidates worth watching.

“You are talking about a number of races that, if Democrats win them, they are going to be very tight,” Skelley said. “If you have a Libertarian getting four or five percent of the vote in Texas or something, and Talarico wins by two, that’s going to be a talking point.”

The opening for Libertarians reflects a broader change in how Americans vote, Tamas said. Voters were once more willing to support candidates from the other major party, but growing hostility toward the other side has made voters less willing to cross party lines.

“A lot of it is negative partisanship,” Tamas said. “It’s hatred of the other side and feeling like the other side is a danger to democracy.”

As a result, Tamas said, Republicans frustrated with their party’s leadership this cycle might be more inclined to turn to a third-party candidate “simply because they absolutely refuse to vote for a Democratic candidate.”

“The Libertarian candidate then produces a way out,” he said. “It’s like, ‘Okay, I’ll vote. I’m not voting for the Republican. I’m not voting for the Democrat. I’ll just pick this other one.’”

articles.title: Hegseth’s future as Pentagon chief at center of lame-duck defense battle
articles.summary: Senate Democrats are quietly floating the ouster of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth after the Nov. 3 election as the political price for cooperation on key...
articles.body:
Senate Democrats are quietly floating the ouster of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth after the Nov. 3 election as the political price for cooperation on key defense-related issues in the post-election lame duck session, and they may have some GOP support to shake-up the Pentagon's leadership, according to Senate sources.

The Defense Department has set recruiting records under Hegseth's leadership and the Pentagon chief appears to have strong support from President Trump, who likes to brag that Hegseth looks like a military leader from "central casting."

But some Republican senators haven't been happy with Hegseth's leadership, especially his ouster of well-respected military leaders such as Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, Army Chief of Staff Randy George, Navy Secretary John Phelan and four-star Gen. Chris Donahue, the top U.S. military officer in Europe.

Now Democrats have significant leverage over Hegseth's future at the Pentagon as they're threatening to hold up emergency defense funding the White House requested in June as well as regular funding for the Defense Department, which expires on Dec. 11.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said that Hegseth's resignation could set the stage for more bipartisan cooperation on must-pass defense bills, such as the National Defense Authorization Act and the annual defense appropriations bill.

Republican sources say that Senate Democrats have already privately floated Hegseth's termination as something that could help muster bipartisan cooperation on filling key vacancies at the Pentagon, such as the positions of Army and Navy secretary left open by the departures of Driscoll and Phelan.

As things now stand, Senate Democrats are threatening to block the defense spending bills and also a waiver that Hung Cao, Trump's nominee to serve as Navy secretary.

Cao needs a special congressional waiver to lead the Navy because federal law requires a seven-year waiting period before former military officers can be confirmed to top Pentagon civilian leadership posts.

Democrats are drawing a hard line on supporting defense funding in the lame-duck session if the military conflict with Iran isn't wrapped up before the end of the year.

"My own view is that if the war is over, then the opportunity for bipartisanship on defense authorization and defense appropriations is there. I think if the war's not over it's going to be extremely difficult," said Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), who is poised to take over as Democratic whip in the next Congress.

Schatz said he was speaking about his own personal view of the prospects of a deal on defense spending.

So far, some key Senate Republicans say they don't see Trump agreeing to push Hegseth out of the job to get cooperation from Democrats on the defense authorization and funding measures in the lame-duck session.

"That's a bridge too far," warned a GOP senator, who requested anonymity to discuss the looming negotiations over breaking the logjam on defense legislation after Election Day.

A senior Pentagon official dismissed the criticism of Hegseth's leadership from Democrats and some key Republicans by pointing to his record of accomplishments over the past 20 months.

"Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump's direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength," the official said in response to jockeying by Democrats to push Hegseth out of his role.

"Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all-time highs. Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way. By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under Secretary Hegseth's leadership than before," the senior official said. "The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary's vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first."

There are growing questions, however, on Capitol Hill whether Trump and Hegseth are fully in sync on several important issues.

Trump recently cancelled Hegseth's plan to run a livestream of the execution of Maj. Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 at a mass shooting at Fort Hood in 2009.

There's also confusion whether Hegseth or other senior Pentagon officials directed a temporary halt to intelligence sharing with Ukraine or ordered the restriction of Ukraine's access to the Starshield satellite-based internet network, without Trump's knowledge and approval.

Four Republican senators — Senate Appropriations Committee Susan Collins (Maine), Sen. John Cornyn (Texas), Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.) and Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) — signed a bipartisan letter last week directing the Defense Department inspector general, Platte Moring, demanding he immediately investigate whether any Pentagon officials "directed" or "authorized" changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine.

Collins has separately faulted Hegseth for not fully anticipating that Iran would be able to shut down most shipping traffic, including nearly a quarter of the world's seaborne oil supply, through the vulnerable Strait of Hormuz in response to U.S. and Israeli attacks.

"For example, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz should have been anticipated. It happened during the Iraq-Iran war and it's an obvious point of leverage but there doesn't seem to have been any plan for it," Collins said last month.

Tillis writes in his new memoir that his decision to cast a deciding vote to confirm Hegseth in January of 2025 is "the biggest regret of my career."

Some Republicans already acknowledge that pushing Hegseth out of his job in the lame-duck session could avoid a messy impeachment battle next year, aside from paving the way for a potential deal on the defense authorization and appropriations bills before Christmas.

"Trump should fire Hegseth to avoid Hegseth's impeachment. It's the honorable thing to do," Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) posted on X, the social media site, Thursday.

The maverick conservative who lost his primary re-election bid earlier this year when Trump endorsed his opponent noted that Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) had to scramble to avoid voting on Hegseth's impeachment before the election.

"The House recessed early to avoid the vote, so I will reintroduce Hegseth articles of impeachment when we return for the lame duck session, regardless of the outcome of the midterm election,"

House Democrats led by Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April.

Democrats in the lower chamber plan to make a Hegseth a top political target next year if they win the majority in next month's election, something that political handicappers project is likely.

Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) told Semafor that impeaching Hegseth should be one of House Democrats' "top three priorities" next year.
