articles.title: Bulldozed trees spike DC tensions: Inside Trump’s takeover of East Potomac Park
articles.summary: A federal judge on Monday will hear testimony from officials in President Trump’s Department of Interior about the administration’s plans for East Potomac Park, a sprawling piece of National Park land that hosts D.C.’s most popular public golf course. Tensions were at an all-time high at East Potomac last week after hundreds of trees were…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Monday will hear testimony from officials in President Trump’s Department of Interior about the administration’s plans for East Potomac Park, a sprawling piece of National Park land that hosts D.C.’s most popular public golf course.

Tensions were at an all-time high at East Potomac last week after hundreds of trees were cut down as the president eyes the location for redevelopment.

A recent order from a U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes halting the work has left a feeling of uncertainty and frustration among golfers, bikers and runners at the park, where daily play continues with massive excavating equipment and half-chopped branches only feet from the fairways and tee boxes.

It was a scene many there had dreaded for weeks after the administration dumped tons of dirt moved from the White House ballroom construction project on the north end of the property months earlier. Some of what the White House left on the property later tested positive for toxic material; it’s been there for months.

Trump has been planning a redevelopment of East Potomac all year, angering golfers by repeatedly flying over the property this summer in Marine One. Trump has enlisted leading golf course architect Tom Fazio to consult on the project.

His vision, the president has told people close to him, is to construct a state of the art 18-hole championship facility capable of hosting professional tournaments and future Ryder Cups.

Trump confirmed his plan in Truth Social post on Sunday, publishing a graphic of a new course design by Fazio and writing that the current conditions at East Potomac are “overgrown, dysfunctional, and unsafe.”

East Potomac will close on Nov. 15, the president said, so work can begin on a renovation project he estimated would take 15 months to complete.

The president’s impending takeover of East Potomac has left the D.C. golf scene in limbo for most of the year after his administration terminated its lease with the National Links Trust, a local nonprofit that had been operating the district’s courses since the coronavirus pandemic.

Under NLT, D.C. public golf became known around the country as a model for affordable, casual play. That’s a rarity in a major metro area known for its elite clubs and a bevy of high-priced private courses.

In May, the NLT said it had struck a deal with the Trump administration allowing the nonprofit to keep operational control of East Potomac until the president’s renovation project was complete.

The NLT in a statement to The Hill on Sunday said all work at East Potomac is being undertaken by the Department of the Interior and National Park Service.

“National Links Trust is in place solely as the operator of the facility in a holdover capacity,” a spokesperson for the nonprofit said in response to a request for comment on Trump’s Truth Social post.

Several East Potomac golfers told The Hill this week they were devastated by the recent tree cutting work and worry a lengthy legal fight could lead to poorer playing conditions.

“To be honest this course got me into golf. It’s very cheap and isn’t pretentious like other clubs so if they raised the price to play here it would be pretty annoying,” golfer Hugo Gowdin said after finishing up a round at East Potomac’s 9-hole short course.

Godwin conceded he can see why Trump has his eye on the property, but East Potomac’s current atmosphere and clientele are part of the facility’s charm, he said.

“It’s really unique in that you can play at a really nice, manicured course but you’re not going to get views of the Washington Monument like this,” he said.

Trump’s vision, which involves essentially bulldozing a sprawling peninsula bisecting the Potomac River that is used daily by thousands of residents and tourists, faces an intensifying legal challenge from local preservationists’ groups and residents.

NPS crews shocked many at East Potomac last week when they showed up unannounced and quickly began tearing down more than 400 trees, including many of the famous cherry trees that bring thousands of tourists to the nation’s capital each spring. Yards away from the work, dozens of confused golfers played on.

Reyes called an emergency hearing less than 48 hours later and admonished the NPS for moving forward with the work. Reyes said the government had lost “all of its credibility” in the case by violating a pervious order she signed this summer forbidding tree cutting at the site while the lawsuit seeking to stop it plays out.

“I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done,” Reyes said, raising her voice at attorneys for the government and telling them to prepare Trump administration officials to testify in the coming weeks.

“I have given the government the benefit of the doubt and every single time I have been clear that I wanted notice,” Reyes said exclaiming she was “furious” over the tree removal.

Major questions about the feasibility and cost of Trump’s plans for East Potomac remain.

A failed seawall that frequently leads to flooding at the park would cost hundreds of millions to repair, and several local voices have raised concern about the need for parking, lodging and traffic that would come with bringing pro golf to downtown D.C.

In his Sunday Truth Social post, Trump said new course would be open to the public and the project to construct it would “create many Jobs, and have a tremendously positive Economic Development impact on Washington, D.C., and the surrounding area.”

In the meantime, players at East Potomac say conditions have gone downhill since Trump announced his plans.

“It seems like they don’t know if they want to put work into it or just let it go. So, it just kind of sucks right now. I mean the driving range is destroyed and the [Trackman] cameras they don’t replace, so we’re just kind of in a waiting period,” said Nolin Boyle, another golfer who played at East Potomac after the tree cutting. “I just kind of wish they would make a decision one way or another.”

Allies of the president have sought to justify the work at East Potomac, arguing it falls in line with the administration’s monthslong beatification efforts impacting major D.C. landmarks like the Reflecting Pool and Kennedy Center.

“I missed the part of the Constitutional Convention that put federal judges in charge of golf course maintenance,” top Trump aide Stephen Miller wrote on social media responding to Reyes’ order. “The Left is endlessly enraged that, after allowing DC to decay for decades, the Trump Administration is making it safe, clean and beautiful.”

Elected Democrats with constituencies in the D.C., Virginia and Maryland metro area say they are consistently hearing from dismayed residents about the work that has already been done and is still planned at East Potomac.

“All we’re hearing is anxiety and anger. The bikers are apoplectic about it and so are the runners. And nobody is talking about what the cost will be, but knowing Donald Trump it’s hard to imagine,” Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) who represents nearby Arlington, Va., told The Hill. “He very much wants to remake D.C. all in his own gilded image and it certainly doesn’t respect the will of Washingtonians.”

Rep. Glen Ivey (D-Md.) said the recent tree cutting could be an episode that fuels Democrats’ appetite for investigating the Trump administration if the party wins back majorities in Congress this fall.

“This is classic Trump moving first and trying to get permission later. But when you cut down over 500 trees, that’s hard to fix,” Ivey said. “There are people who get prosecuted criminally for these kinds of things. It’s inexcusable for them to do this knowing there were objections from the public. When you’ve got this kind of reckless conduct from the president and his minions, there’s gotta be ways to rein that in.”

The Federal Trade Commission is reportedly preparing a major probe of leading online sportsbooks like FanDuel and DraftKings over their aggressive advertising and marketing strategies. News of such scrutiny from federal regulators comes as the Trump administration has increasingly sided with prediction markets, the online sportsbooks’ largest competitors, as those platforms face legal fights in various states across the country. The NFL, which does billions in business with online sportsbooks every year, notably petitioned the Supreme Court earlier this month asking it to clear the way for stricter state regulations of prediction market platforms, potentially setting up a showdown between the country’s most popular sports league and federal government over what constitutes sports gambling in the U.S.

A new memo unsealed as part of former NFL coach Brian Flores’ lawsuit against the NFL shows one search firm referring to him as “polished and a good presenter despite growing up in Brownsville, Brooklyn.” Flores is suing league owners over what he says is a violating of its Rooney Rule requiring the consideration of minorities for head coaching positions. Flores’ lawyers say they expect more documents to come out proving race was a factor in him being passed over for coaching positions.

The NCAA filed a lawsuit this week against the state of Ohio and Governor Mike DeWine (R) after he surprised some in the college sports world with an executive order dictating that revamped NCAA rules put in place by Congress cannot trump state law governing college athletics. The order flies in the face of the NCAA’s effort to get Congress to pass the “Protect College Sports Act,” which is backed by the Big Ten and Ohio State University, the largest NCAA member school and a top football program in DeWine’s state.

Jocks on The Hill: Rep. Dale Strong (R-Ala.)

Rep. Dale Strong (R-Ala.), who saved a man from a car wreck in his home district while serving as a county official before being elected to Congress, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“I played high school football so I would have to say football is my favorite but I like baseball also.”

“In Alabama we don’t have pro sports. It’s all about Auburn and Alabama and I’m a big SEC fan. Both my children graduated from Auburn and my wife, my sister graduated from Alabama, my brother from Auburn. So we got a house divided but we love SEC football. I’m War Eagle.”

Is there an athlete you admired growing up?

“Oh, it’s Bo Jackson. The best two-sport athlete to ever play the game and I’ve met him several times. I know Bo and he was not just an athlete but an example the way he carried himself. He went through some hard times with the broken hip and he never questioned that injury he just said it was his path. So Bo Jackson is my favorite by far.”

Hate is a strong word but is there a team you love to root against?

“I don’t think I’d say I root against any one team but I am definitely let’s say a Southeastern Conference advocate.”

Nicole Noren, a longtime producer at ESPN, quit the network in protest over the outlet’s ties to sports gambling platforms and gave an extensive interview to the Columbia Journalism Review during which she told a personal story about gambling addiction in her family, saying, “I’m not going to have blood on my hands.”

Former NFL star Tyreek Hill is reportedly talking to several NFL teams about a potential comeback, prompting The Athletic’s Adam Kilgore to publish a thorough look at Hill’s long history of legal issues, writing the explosive wide receiver’s career “has been an exercise in how far a football player can stretch a second chance.”

The Financial Times’ Sujeet Indap has done some great reporting on the LIV Golf financial debacle and the league’s ongoing bankruptcy proceedings after the Saudi Foreign Wealth Fund pulled its money from the venture. As the company attempts to cobble together funding for a potential second act, Indap explores a direct but complicated question: “Can a financier really revive LIV Golf?”

articles.title: It took 3 months to get inside this massive Texas data center — here’s what we saw
articles.summary: Compass Datacenters CEO Chris Crosby says the data center boom is fueling blue-collar jobs for electricians, mechanics and technicians in Red Oak, Texas.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: As massive data centers rise across the country to power America's artificial intelligence boom, one of the industry's biggest builders is making the case that the benefits extend far beyond the technology inside. During an exclusive tour of Compass Datacenters' sprawling campus in Red Oak, Texas, Fox News Digital got a rare look inside the infrastructure behind the nation's growing appetite for computing. Getting inside took roughly three months of approvals. Once on site, Fox News Digital passed through six layers of security and suited up in personal protective equipment before entering the facility, where photos and recording devices were prohibited. Beyond the checkpoints, the interior was remarkably clean and surprisingly quiet, with little of the industrial noise one might expect from an operation running around the clock. Inside, rows of towering server racks stretched across the spotless floor surrounded by the electrical and cooling systems needed to keep the equipment operating. At Red Oak, Compass uses a closed-loop cooling system that recirculates coolant rather than continuously drawing water to cool the equipment. DATA CENTER CEO SHARES THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM Compass CEO Chris Crosby, a North Texas native, said the Red Oak campus has not used water for cooling since it began operating. "We haven't used water since inception," Crosby said, noting the importance of conserving the region's resources. "Water is precious in North Texas." Beyond cooling, security is another major consideration for facilities housing vast amounts of computing infrastructure. Crosby said the extensive security is not about keeping the facilities secret, but rather protecting the sensitive information and critical infrastructure housed inside. "Hacking is real, attacks on infrastructure are real," Crosby said. "If people knew that a bank or a government was operating at a particular facility, they could infiltrate that facility. So that's why the levels of security are so high at our campuses." The campus, roughly 20 miles south of Dallas, will eventually include 10 data center buildings spanning roughly 2.6 million square feet. A Schneider Electric manufacturing facility and a workforce training center operated in partnership with Texas State Technical College are also located on the campus. AMERICA’S NEW BLUE-COLLAR JOB BOOM IS ONE NOBODY SAW COMING — AND IT’S JUST GETTING STARTED Crosby said the development offers a glimpse at an often-overlooked side of America's data center boom: blue-collar jobs. "Data centers are where the economic engine is going to be going forward," Crosby told Fox News Digital, pointing to the jobs, economic activity and tax revenue generated by the industry. Roughly 600 people work for Compass at the campus, while Schneider Electric employs about 300 more, according to Crosby. Thousands of construction workers have also cycled through the development since work began in 2019. And the company says it needs more. "We can't get enough people into this career," Crosby said. That demand helped spur the creation of MEI Pathways, a workforce development program built in partnership with Texas State Technical College. The $12.6 million training facility offers a 12-week program aimed at preparing electricians, mechanics and technicians for jobs in the industry. Building data centers also requires an array of skilled trades, including carpenters, welders and concrete workers. A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES "There was a war on blue-collar jobs for a long time — everybody had to get a four-year degree," Crosby said. "I'm so glad that's over with." Compass has worked with local officials on roads, sewer and other infrastructure and donated $15 million toward a new animal shelter after Ellis County's previous shelter arrangement ended. The investments come as Texas grapples with how to accommodate the enormous electricity demands accompanying the industry's growth while protecting the reliability of its power grid. "I am tired of the elitism that this doesn't create jobs," he said.

articles.title: Should journos praise themselves for correcting their own mistakes?
articles.summary: No.
articles.body:
Allow me to introduce to your vocabulary the “self-congratulatory correction.” Few things demonstrate so well the excessive self-regard that some in the news media have for themselves and their industry.

You may recall the particulars: A news organization or journalist bungles a story and then issues a correction seemingly designed to make sure everyone knows they are still superior to the targets of their reporting.

Although this was much more of a fad during the first Trump administration, it still happens. People in media treat the mere act of correcting their own mistakes — one of the most basic requirements in any information-based profession — as proof of their own virtue.

MS NOW’s Ken Dilanian really stepped in it last week when he misreported that FBI Director Kash Patel had just landed in Russia. The problem: Patel was not in Russia. He was in Virginia, speaking at a public event.

Dilanian had bad information, and it was too good to check.

With egg on his face, the MS NOW reporter eventually issued an on-air correction. But rather than let it go at just admitting a mistake, he added the following: “We regret this error, and we are transparent about when we make errors.”

Well, yes — why wouldn’t he be transparent about it? Don’t you owe your readers at least that much? Isn’t that the bare minimum?

This sort of self-congratulation for failure was much more common — and just as insufferable — during Trump’s first term, when the president’s perfidy was often confused for a blanket absolution for journalistic malpractice.

In 2020, then-CNN analyst Chris Cillizza cited the mere existence of editor’s notes and corrections as proof of the media’s supposed superiority, especially when compared to the bad man who says false things.

“The very fact that we issue public corrections — in the most transparent way possible — is a testament to our commitment to getting it right,” Cillizza wrote. “Now, contrast that approach to how President Trump and the White House operate. Trump, according to The Washington Post’s Fact-Checker blog, has said more than 18,000 false or misleading things in his first 1,170 days in office—an average of 15 incorrect claims every single day he has been president.”

Speaking of the Washington Post Fact-Checker , its former chief, Glenn Kessler, wrote an entire post in 2018 simply titled “The news media does apologize for mistakes, unlike the White House.”

That same year, the New York Times issued a minor correction, updating its estimate of a Trump rally from 1,000 to roughly 5,500 attendees. The story’s author, Julie Hirschfeld Davis, eventually tweeted a correction, writing [emphasis added]: “President [Trump] is correct about his crowd last night. My estimate was way off, and we have corrected our story to reflect the fire marshal’s estimate of 5,500 people. When we get it wrong, we say so.”

Why do they keep stressing this final point, as if they deserve a medal for not grossly misleading their readers?

Earlier, in 2017, then-Washington Post commentator Philip Bump warned specifically that the news media were just too darned honest for their own good. Their dedication to correcting the record, he said, was opening them up to unfair attacks.

““Donald Trump was eminently prepared to launch an asymmetric warfare campaign against the institutions of American democracy, nowhere more effectively than against the media,” Bump complained in an article that ran under the syndicated headline “ Unlike Trump, media owns its mistakes .” “His career — part salesman, part showman, part hustler — taught him a key lesson that, as it turns out, was as effective against the media as an IED could be against a military caravan: Never admit you’re wrong.”

Remember: during the years these pieces were written, major newsrooms attempted the Herculean task of proving fantasies were reality. They poured an absurd amount of time, effort, manpower, and resources into proving a conspiracy theory alleging that Vladimir Putin had installed Trump as U.S. president, going so far as to award themselves major honors for a story that was ultimately as phony as a three-dollar bill.

Just this month, former New York Times executive editor Jill Abramson praised New York Times columnist Nikole Hannah-Jones for questioning her own decision to sabotage her daughter’s education in the name of progressive idealism .

Hannah-Jones wrote recently that maybe it was a mistake to enroll her daughter in an infamously crummy school when she could afford better. In response, Abramson gushed over Jones’s bravery, declaring “‘I was wrong’ are the most powerful words we have.” She then segued (of course) into unfavorable comparisons to Trump, who provided a good education for his children.

As for Hannah-Jones and anyone else in media willing to concede fault, Abramson warns their honesty will be weaponized against them.

“I worry that it makes the paper an even bigger target for President Trump,” Abramson warned. “Trump is utterly incapable of admitting he was ever wrong.” Incredibly, that’s where her mind went — to Trump; not to the tragedy of a bright young girl whose childhood opportunities were sacrificed over a decade on the altar of self-centered virtue-signaling .

Abramson also cheered the relatively recent phenomenon of newsrooms being more willing to admit when they are at fault.

She is right that some major news outlets still drag their feet in this area. This includes ABC News, which ran a false story earlier this month about companies tied to Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump — that they had secured more than $6 billion in government contracts.

The story disappeared the same day it was published, with no editor’s note or clarification. After more than 24 hours of nothing, ABC restored a version of the story with a different headline, a different thesis, key claims removed, and the $6 billion figure completely missing. Even the name of the story’s original author disappeared, his byline swapped for the generic “ABC NEWS.” That’s one way of getting around a full retraction.

Our first job is to get it right — so already on that count you have failed when you issue a correction. That admission of error is needed, but it is not grounds for self-praise — rather, it is the lowest possible bar you must clear to salvage your remaining credibility with readers.

To attach your correction to a sense of self-superiority is gross and hubristic and even suggests an alarming lack of contrition. It is positively — if I may say it — Trumpian.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: SCOTT WALKER: Just three votes on one ballot helped decide Wisconsin’s future
articles.summary: Tyler August won his Wisconsin State Assembly primary by just three votes in a recount, launching one of the state's most consequential careers.
articles.body: Three votes. That is the margin that helped launch one of the most consequential political careers in modern Wisconsin state government. In September 2010, Tyler August was a 27-year-old candidate running in a six-way Republican primary for an open seat in the Wisconsin State Assembly. When election night ended, it appeared he had lost. Adam Gibbs was reported ahead by four votes. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS THE HOUSE FALLS, THE SENATE STAYS IN PLAY Then came the recount. When it was finished, August had won 1,760 votes to Gibbs’ 1,757. Three votes. Out of more than 7,300 cast. Fewer people than fit around most kitchen tables separated winning from losing. GEORGIA VOTERS SET EARLY-VOTING RECORD AS MIDTERM ELECTIONS HEAT UP August went on to win the general election that November. Sixteen years later, he serves as majority leader of the Wisconsin State Assembly, one of the most powerful positions in state government. Think about everything that had to pass through that three-vote doorway first. Every vote he has cast in the legislature. Every bill he has introduced. Every budget he has helped shape. Every negotiation, committee assignment and leadership decision that came afterward. Every Wisconsin family, worker or business affected by legislation enacted during his time in office. None of it happens the same way if that primary ends differently. That is the part we tend to forget when we say our vote "doesn’t matter." August went on to win the general election that November. Sixteen years later, he serves as majority leader of the Wisconsin State Assembly, one of the most powerful positions in state government. We imagine elections as enormous things. Millions of people. Billions of dollars. Television ads, polling averages, consultants, candidates and endless political noise. Against all of that, one person standing in a voting booth can feel almost comically insignificant. But elections are not actually decided by "the electorate." They are decided by individual people, one ballot at a time. And my home state of Wisconsin offers a remarkable example of just how thin the distance between two outcomes can be. FOX NEWS POLL: COST-OF-LIVING CONCERNS WEIGH ON GOP IN MIDTERMS In the 2020 presidential election, more than 3.2 million Wisconsinites cast ballots. The final margin was 20,682 votes. Only Georgia and Arizona had narrower margins by percentage, with their presidential contests decided by just 11,779 and 10,457 votes, respectively. Four years later, more than 3.4 million Wisconsinites voted, and the presidential margin was 29,397, making Wisconsin the closest state in the country by percentage of votes cast. Those numbers sound large until you compare them with the millions of ballots cast. Then there is Tyler August. Three. Wisconsin's experience offers a lesson for voters across America: No election should be treated as a foregone conclusion. And the consequences stretch far beyond which name appears on an office door. GINGRICH: NOBODY SHOULD ASSUME THIS ELECTION IS OVER State and local governments across the country make decisions every year about taxes, regulations, housing, licensing, education, infrastructure, employment rules and the cost of doing business. Those decisions determine how easy it is to open a storefront, hire another employee, build a home, expand a farm or invest in a community. In the 2020 presidential election, more than 3.2 million Wisconsinites cast ballots. The final margin was 20,682 votes. Only Georgia and Arizona had narrower margins by percentage, with their presidential contests decided by just 11,779 and 10,457 votes, respectively. Free enterprise does not exist separately from government policy. The rules government writes shape the environment in which people take risks, build businesses and create opportunity. Which means the people who write those rules matter. And the people who choose them matter too. Voting is sometimes talked about as an expression of personal identity. Increasingly, politics itself feels that way. Pick a team, wear the jersey, argue about it online. But a ballot is much more practical than that. It is one of the few moments when every citizen gets the exact same unit of political power. One person. One vote. The business owner with 40 employees gets one. The college student voting for the first time gets one. The retiree who has voted in every election for 50 years gets one. So does the person who nearly stays home because the weather is lousy, the line might be long, they have errands to run, or they assume everyone else will decide the outcome anyway. The margin between having political power and never getting the opportunity to exercise it can be three people. And somewhere in southeastern Wisconsin are voters who helped create that margin. They probably went home that night without feeling particularly powerful. Free enterprise does not exist separately from government policy. The rules government writes shape the environment in which people take risks, build businesses and create opportunity. They were. On Nov. 3, Americans across the country will make thousands of similarly unremarkable choices. Get up early or hit snooze. Stop at the polling place or drive past it. Return the absentee ballot or leave it sitting on the kitchen counter. Most of us will never know precisely what depended on our decision. That is the point. Democracy asks us to participate before we know whether our vote will be one of the millions or one of the three. Whether you live in Wisconsin or somewhere else in America, the first step is knowing when, where and how to vote. Check your registration status, find your polling place and make a plan for Nov. 3. Election information and registration requirements are available through your state or local election office. So, vote for the candidates you believe will make your community, your state and your country stronger. Vote for the policies and principles you want represented in your state capital and Washington. But vote. Because somewhere in Wisconsin history are voters who helped create a three-vote margin, proving that the difference between "my vote probably won’t matter" and changing the direction of government can be almost impossibly small. articles.title: Trump tests GOP resolve on Russia, Ukraine
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Zelensky raises pressure ▪ No Kings protest as early vote starts ▪ Experts see weak measles messaging ▪ Trump endorses Netanyahu Republicans are growing increasingly frustrated over President Trump’s recent moves that have advantaged Russia on the battlefield at the cost of the U.S.’s ally Ukraine, but whether they can force the…
articles.body:
Republicans are growing increasingly frustrated over President Trump ’s recent moves that have advantaged Russia on the battlefield at the cost of the U.S.’s ally Ukraine, but whether they can force the issue in Congress remains to be seen.

The president’s executive order signed Friday to waive sanctions against Russia, just days before they took effect, quickly fueled backlash from Democrats and some Republicans.

The sanctions were to be implemented under a law that passed Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), a staunch Trump ally and ardent Ukraine supporter.

“It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), one of the more vocal Trump critics within the GOP, said in a post on the social platform X.

“Lindsey would be appalled,” wrote Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

Trump defended his decision to waive sanctions in a Truth Social post on Sunday, arguing that it keeps Russia at the negotiating table. He said he could reverse course at any time.

“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he said.

Republican leaders intentionally gave the president broad discretion over the sanctions in order to get the White House’s support for the bill. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told Fox News on Sunday that Trump’s waiver was “the right decision.”

The move is one of a few the administration has made in recent days that critics say are only contributing to furthering Russian President Vladimir Putin ‘s war machine.

Trump’s deal with Putin to import Russian diesel fuel into the U.S. has been met with similar pushback across the political spectrum.

This has come while Ukrainian officials have reported they’ve lost access to SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield technology, which has been key to Ukraine’s communications and drone operations during the war.

Both Elon Musk , who owns SpaceX, and the White House have denied responsibility for the interruption to Ukraine’s access. The Telegraph has reported that Musk came to Trump with the idea , while a source familiar with the discussion told Axios that Trump didn’t push back on it.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told NBC News’s Kristen Welker Starlink had been “deblocked” in an interview that aired Sunday on “Meet the Press.”

“We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.”

He’s been seeking to ramp up pressure on the Trump administration in recent days to stand by his country, warning of dire consequences if Ukraine is abandoned.

“If United States will support Putin, I mean, it’s unbelievable, it’s tragedy, it’s historic mistake and big tragedy. That’s why I think that I don’t want to live in illusions, but I think that we have to be pragmatic,” he told Welker.

The administration’s Russia-friendly posture has rallied a growing chorus of House Republicans to use their leverage ahead of an expected battle over additional funding for the Pentagon in Congress following the midterms, The Hill’s Mike Lillis and Filip Timotija report .

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) warned that none of Trump’s legislative agenda will pass through Congress during the lame-duck session unless the president takes action to punish Russia. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) threatened funding for agencies “if they’re not doing their jobs.”

“There’s going to be enough pressure from the Hill that the admin recognizes that they need to back off, to some degree, if they actually want to get something done,” a House GOP aide said.

Republicans also don’t seem to all be taking the administration’s word that it wasn’t responsible for the disruption to Ukraine’s Starlink access.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated Saturday that the administration didn’t order it slowed but it “sort of happened.”

Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), a member of the House Armed Services Committee, said on CBS News’s “Face the Nation” that the explanation is “absolutely not” sufficient .

“This is something where there needs to be” a congressional investigation, Turner said.

Sens. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) and Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) are pushing a deal to give Ukraine access to Starshield over Russia in exchange for Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian petroleum infrastructure, which Trump has blamed for worsening the global energy crisis.

Cramer told Margaret Brennan this would allow Ukraine to “go deep into Russia and attack their attackers, in other words, their launch facilities, kill the archer, not the arrows,” during an appearance on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”

Even Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), the sister of the late senator, broke with the president over the sanctions waiver, saying she planned to discuss the matter with him when he visits South Carolina for a rally this week.

“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia … because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia,” she told The Associated Press, stopping short of criticizing Trump directly.

▪ The Hill : The Memo: Ukraine’s slide into crisis sharpens questions for Trump.

▪ The Hill : Ukraine faces grim question on if it can go on without the U.S.

CALL FOR NOMINATIONS : The Hill is currently collecting nominations for its annual Top Lobbyists list, made up of the most influential folks in Washington. Know a lobbyist who moved the needle this year? Nominate them for The Hill’s Top Lobbyists here by Nov. 6.

Shawn Oliver, the GOP’s lieutenant governor nominee in Massachusetts, has suspended his campaign after he was arrested and charged with one count of operating under the influence following a car crash late Saturday night. Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue had called on his running mate to step aside.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed four of his country’s service members were killed in a fire that broke out at a military base in Alberta. An additional 39 people were hospitalized, including at least 19 in critical condition. Officials are investigating the cause.

Trump rolled out a plan for a new golf course at East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C., on Sunday, showing a proposed course that would take up much of the island that the park sits on. A federal judge last week ordered the administration to stop work on the park after hundreds of trees were cut down.

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., arrives before Dr. Heidi Overton testifies at her nomination hearing to become the commissioner of Food and Drug Administration at the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee on Capitol Hill, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib)

ROLLING ON : The president is expanding on his midterm blitz this week as he makes a final pitch to voters throughout the country to keep Republicans in power in Congress.

Trump will make a different stop every day this week, starting today in Kansas, where Sen. Roger Marshall (R) is facing a surprisingly competitive race despite Democrats not having won a Senate seat there in more than 90 years. Polls show Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton essentially neck and neck.

Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted the race to “toss-up” last week, noting that a “full-on Republican rescue operation” seems to be underway for Marshall.

Following the stop today, Trump will travel to North Carolina on Tuesday, South Carolina on Wednesday, Iowa on Thursday, Florida on Friday, Georgia on Saturday and Michigan on Sunday.

Both sides are rolling out the big guns. Former President Obama will campaign with Michigan Democratic candidates on Saturday, while former President Clinton will campaign for Florida Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Jolly on Tuesday.

▪ The Hill Insider : This Week: Michigan Senate debate, Trump rallies.

▪ The Hill : Abdul El-Sayed criticizes implication of Muslim Brotherhood question.

TO THE STREETS : Thousands of “No Kings” protests were held over the weekend as part of a national “day of action” demonstrating against the president as the early voting window starts throughout the country.

The protests were the fourth iteration of the demonstrations put on by the No Kings Coalition during Trump’s second term, bringing millions onto streets nationwide.

In Washington, D.C., protesters marched from the White House to the Capitol holding signs such as “Your vote is your voice” and “Pro-American, anti-Trump.”

The protests come as Trump critics and pro-democracy advocates have expressed concern about the president possibly seeking to interfere with the midterms to ensure Republicans stay in control of Congress. The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch and Mike Lillis report on how outside good-government groups are scrambling to protect the results from any outside interference.

Insiders can read more about the organizations’ plan to safeguard elections here .

▪ NPR : No Kings draws crowds with early-voting focus.

PREGAME TRAGEDY : A U.S. Air Force member died Saturday after falling while attempting to rappel from the rafters before a football game between the University of Texas at San Antonio (UTSA) and the Navy.

The service member was taken to a local hospital, where he died. He was one of four scheduled to appear during a pregame rappelling demonstration during UTSA’s annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans game.

An investigation is underway into what happened. The service member, whose identity hasn’t been publicly revealed yet, was assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2, The Associated Press reported.

The president will sign an executive order at 11 a.m. He will travel to Wichita, Kan., to deliver remarks at 7 p.m. EDT before returning to the White House.

The Senate will meet at 9 a.m. for a pro forma session.

The House will convene at 10 a.m. for a pro forma session.

A nurse prepares a combination measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine for a patient at a pediatrics clinic in Easley, S.C., on March 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Mary Conlon)

CALL FOR HELP : Infectious disease experts say clearer communication is needed from top health leaders as officials attempt to get a growing measles outbreak under control.

More than 4,000 measles cases have been confirmed nationwide so far, and the number of deaths appears to have already doubled compared to last year. Money has been sent to state and local health departments to counter the outbreaks, but The Hill’s Joseph Choi reports that experts say clear guidance from federal authorities has been lacking.

“I do think that a national message can be crafted to encompass a more broad kind of acceptance of people’s vaccine hesitancy,” said Jeanne Marrazzo , the CEO of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “We just haven’t really seen that because, again, I don’t think we’ve seen a full-throated endorsement or explanation of why the vaccine right now is so critical.”

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has sent roughly $100 million in additional funding to state, local and tribal health departments, supporting vaccinations, prevention and disease detection efforts. The agency also said it would send additional support to Pennsylvania, which has the highest number of cases in the country.

But guidance or vocal endorsements of measles vaccines and mitigation efforts have been lacking.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz hasn’t said much about the outbreak. She did tell a local Atlanta news outlet that measles is the “most contagious disease” and reiterated the vaccine is “safe and effective.”

But specialists said a stronger messaging campaign would go a long way.

▪ The Hill : CDC sends ‘disease detective’ to Pennsylvania.

▪ The Hill : Health insurance is the sleeper midterm issue.

President Trump, right, poses for a photo with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu before he boards Air Force One at Ben Gurion International Airport on Oct. 13, 2025, near Tel Aviv, as Israeli President Isaac Herzog watches at left. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci)

BACKING BIBI : Trump declared his support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday ahead of Israel’s critical legislative elections next week.

Trump said in a post on Truth Social directed to the “Great People of Israel” that Netanyahu is a “Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting” Iran.

Some tensions have flared up between Trump and Netanyahu in recent months over how to conduct the Iran war and the broader Middle East conflict. Trump confirmed in June that he called Netanyahu “f—cking crazy” during a heated phone conversation over his frustrations with Israel’s military operations in Lebanon.

Still, the two leaders have been key allies for years. The Iran war began at the end of February with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes.

Netanyahu is set to face Israeli voters for the first time since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks next Tuesday, Oct. 27. His reputation as Israel’s best defender against its enemies took a potentially mortal hit following the deadliest attack on the country in its history. His critics have argued he is to blame for the intelligence failure that allowed the attacks to happen.

Polls show a close race between Netanyahu’s coalition and the opposition bloc led by former general Gadi Eisenkot . Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having been in power for more than 15 years apart from a roughly yearlong period out of power.

“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump said. “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself. Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!”

▪ The Hill : Mike Huckabee condemns Israeli settlers’ attack on photojournalist.

▪ The Hill : Israeli filmmakers bring counter ‘NAZA’ programming to Capitol.

We didn’t protect children from social media — we have another chance with AI , Kris Perry writes in The Hill.

Divided we fall: Violent partisanship and the threat to national security , Douglas MacKinnon writes in The Hill.

Former Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes leaves federal court in San Jose, Calif., March 17, 2023. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu, File)

And finally … Filmmaker and comedian Nathan Fielder ’s documentary about disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes has drawn 2,000 sold-out shows so far during its limited run across the U.S.

The documentary, entitled “You Can See Everything,” was released over the weekend, depicting Holmes just before she was to report to prison in 2023. Forbes estimated the film grossed $15 million during the weekend.

Holmes was seen as a possible next Steve Jobs after pioneering technology that could supposedly test for a wide array of diseases with a small amount of blood from a simple finger prick. But her company collapsed as she was convicted of fraud charges for misleading investors.

Holmes is serving a more than 10-year prison sentence but was reportedly approved last month to be moved to a halfway house next year.

articles.title: AI’s future is brighter than its headlines
articles.summary: We have integrated powerful and potentially dangerous technologies into our lives before.
articles.body:
A technology that could do more to improve our lives than anything invented in decades is being demonized to the public as something that might wipe us out, taking our jobs and even ending humanity.

Researchers recently left leading laboratories with warnings of catastrophe. One Anthropic researcher puts the odds at above 10 percent of AI killing everyone within a decade . Attach a percentage to the apocalypse, and speculation starts to sound like a scientific finding.

Apparently, we’re all doomed. But I don’t buy it. Even if the negative headlines are the ones that get clicks , I believe AI will leave us considerably better off.

We have heard similar predictions before. In 1985, some warned that Excel would eliminate accountants. Since then, we have added about 600,000 new accounting jobs . In 1995, Ethernet pioneer Bob Metcalfe predicted a “catastrophic collapse” of the internet the following year. When it failed to happen, he put a copy of his column in a blender and literally ate his words .

Y2K was supposed to end the world as we knew it , causing failures in banking and power because of a date change. Midnight came and went — the apocalypse did not.

In each case, technologies that were supposed to make human beings useless helped make us richer, healthier and more capable. We didn’t just survive technological progress — we built better lives with it.

Global output per person has risen many times over since industrialization . Electricity, refrigeration, sanitation, and medicine all transformed ordinary life. Global life expectancy rose from roughly 32 years in 1900 to about 73 in 2023 . Literacy spread . Poverty fell . In many countries, working hours fell substantially, giving people more leisure time. Progress wasn’t always neat and orderly, but it was real.

Most of us would hate living in the world our great-grandparents knew. We take it for granted every time we turn on a light, open a refrigerator or get an infection treated.

Of course, progress does cause lost livelihoods. But eliminating tasks is not the same as eliminating the need for people . Many jobs were replaced with higher-quality, better-paying jobs. More productive workers can do things that weren’t previously possible or worth trying. We find it much easier to name the jobs a machine might replace than the ones that don’t exist yet.

In fairness, AI’s speed of adoption makes that adjustment harder compared to previous technological revolutions. Workers cannot retrain at the speed of a software-release schedule. That is a serious problem to solve, but not evidence that the whole enterprise ends badly.

This fearmongering has many of the frontier labs calling for increased regulation to mitigate the potential negative effects of AI. However, the cost of complying with additional rules can fall unevenly across an industry. Consider the same compliance bill landing on the desks of a global corporation and a five-person startup. For one, it may be a routine expense. For the other, it may mean not hiring the next engineer. Safety standards can support more trustworthy products ; fixed compliance costs can also change who can afford to compete.

There is a name for an industry gaining undue influence over its own oversight: regulatory capture . The history of banking offers examples. For AI, the practical questions are what a rule prevents, what compliance costs and which firms can pay. Even a rule with a genuine safety benefit can leave customers with fewer suppliers, less competition and innovation, and higher prices.

Ultimately, the marketplace will determine which products people find useful enough to keep using. Does the tool work? Is it reliable? Is it worth the money? A customer doesn’t owe a technology company loyalty just because it has a famous founder. Competition gives that customer somewhere else to go and gives a startup a chance to win the business. When only the big boys can afford to play, those choices shrink.

And this race does not stop at America’s borders. The U.S. and China are competing for leadership in AI, with enormous commercial and strategic stakes. A rule adopted in Washington does not automatically bind a developer in Beijing. Who builds the technology will help determine whose products businesses depend on, where investment goes and which countries develop the next generation of companies. America is not the only country deciding what happens next.

Meanwhile, the work that makes me optimistic is already happening. AI is helping scientists predict protein structures and molecular interactions , identify promising antibiotic compounds and test ways to predict which cancer drugs will work for individual patients . These are early advances, but they concern diseases that have defeated us for decades. They deserve more than passing mention between extinction warnings.

At one company, AI-assisted customer-support staff resolved 15 percent more issues per hour on average , with bigger gains among less experienced workers. For all the talk of making people obsolete, people here are getting better at their jobs.

AI is also helping researchers develop better forecasts of floods and wildfire risks . For a family in danger, an earlier warning could mean time to get out. For someone waiting to hear whether a cancer treatment will work, a better way to match drugs to patients could mean another chance. That’s what I have in mind when I talk about AI changing lives: better medicine, less drudgery and opportunities no one can yet imagine.

Yes, these systems need to be tested and monitored . But we have integrated powerful and potentially dangerous technologies into our lives before. Nuclear energy can power a city, even if nuclear weapons can destroy one. The capacity to do harm is real, but it’s not the whole story. That is up to us — the humans in the room.

Dr. Aaron Poynton is executive director of the American Society for AI and chief revenue officer of Applied General Intelligence. His views do not necessarily reflect those of these or other organizations.

articles.title: Don’t let history repeat: The next Congress must end the Iran War
articles.summary: The next Congress must stop the war if President Trump hasn’t done so before January. But that won’t happen unless voters elect representatives on Nov. 3 with enough principle and spine to credibly threaten to remove him.
articles.body:
For many obvious reasons, America needs an aggressive Congress to emerge from the November elections ready to restore the government’s balance of power. If the Iran War is still underway, one of the new Congress’s first jobs should be to end it.

President Trump says he won’t resume strikes against Iran before the elections . It is not clear what he plans for afterward. But in addition to usurping Congress’s war powers, hurting the economy and costing U.S. and Iranian lives, this war of choice violates a sacred contract between commanders-in-chief and American families: the assurance that our sons and daughters will be sent to war only when there is a clear and present danger to national security and no other option but the military.

Instead, Trump’s greed, personal grievances, ego and failure to learn from history all appear to play a role in this war.

Greed: CNBC reports that Trump has holdings in oil and gas companies . His nine largest holdings earned him as much as $4.4 million during the first six months of the war. CNBC found “no evidence” that Trump or his investment managers used advance knowledge in the stock trades or allowed them to influence policy. But it is one of the many examples in which Trump has created the appearance, if not the reality, of conflicted interests.

Trump’s sons, who own investments in multiple defense-related companies, have reportedly collected billions of dollars in defense contracts since their father became president again. No public evidence shows illegality, but the investments create another appearance of conflicted interest, especially with the Pentagon planning to spend more than $1 trillion as it scrambles to replenish depleted stocks of munitions and equipment and repair damages to its bases in the Gulf.

Personal grievance : Trump traded a diplomatic solution — the Obama-era deal with Iran to limit its nuclear program — for warfare. He pulled the U.S. out of the deal , citing specific policy objections. But he was also said to be motivated by his personal dislike for former President Barack Obama. In a leaked diplomatic cable, the British ambassador called Trump’s position “an act of diplomatic vandalism, seemingly for ideological and personality reasons.”

Ego: Several foreign-policy experts, including Brookings’s Robert Kagan , believe that Trump’s objectives in Iran are unachievable. But Trump has repeatedly shown, including during the 2020 election and the riot at the Capitol that followed on Jan. 6, 2021, that he is unwilling or unable to admit defeat . With widely varying accounts from the Pentagon and independent sources, we aren’t sure how many U.S. soldiers have died in the war so far. Civilian deaths are estimated in the thousands .

The Vietnam War taught Americans the price of delaying peace. Richard Nixon ran for president in 1968, promising to end the Vietnam War. When incumbent President Lyndon Johnson nearly brokered a truce between North and South Vietnam, which Johnson hoped would help Hubert Humphrey beat Nixon in the upcoming presidential election, Nixon had a messenger tell South Vietnam to wait, promising it would get a better deal under his presidency. Johnson’s peace initiative collapsed. Johnson privately called it “treason.”

Nixon’s presidential papers show that he entered office acknowledging that the war could not be won militarily . Yet he continued the war and ordered military operations that he kept from Congress. He was concerned about U.S. credibility, South Vietnam’s survival and “peace with honor.” But tapes and documents show that Nixon also sustained the war to keep South Vietnam’s government from collapsing and affecting his 1972 reelection campaign.

During the four years between Nixon’s intervention in Johnson’s peace process and the 1972 election, more than 20,000 U.S. troops were killed, more than 100,000 were wounded, and over a million Vietnamese were reported killed — the cost of a president who “couldn’t let go of a failed war.”

Nixon biographer John Farrell concluded, “We must now weigh apparently criminal behavior that, given the human lives at stake and the decade of carnage that followed in Southeast Asia, may be more reprehensible than anything Nixon did in Watergate.”

Ignoring history : The Vietnam War also taught some tough lessons about modern warfare. Gen. Colin Powell codified several in his Powell Doctrine. It instructs that America should use military force only as a last resort when vital national security interests are at risk, objectives are clear, risks and costs are thoroughly analyzed, there is a plausible exit strategy, and the war has strong domestic and international support. Trump ignored all of it.

The next Congress must stop the war if Trump hasn’t done so before January. But that won’t happen unless voters elect representatives on Nov. 3 with enough principle and spine to credibly threaten to remove him. The war is in Iran, but the ball is now in the electorate’s court.

William S. Becker is co-editor of and a contributor to “Democracy Unchained: How to Rebuild Government for the People,” and a contributor to “Democracy in a Hotter Time.” He previously served as a senior official in the Wisconsin Department of Justice. He is currently executive director of the Presidential Climate Action Project.

articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) said she would rather keep sanctions on Russia after President Trump signed an executive order to waive the penalties.

“The president and I share the same goal, which is to end the war, get gas and diesel prices down, and the sanctions bill is one of the tools we can use to do that. It’s up to him whether or not he chooses to use it,” she said Saturday in an interview with The Associated Press, referring to Trump’s upcoming visit to South Carolina.

“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia to end the war and get the gas prices low, because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia,” she added.

The president has defended the move , which is allowed under Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanction Russia and Iran Act. He signed the law, which was named after the senator’s late brother, in September.

The freshman senator, who was endorsed by Trump, succeeded her brother Lindsey after his unexpected death in July. The late Republican, a vocal war hawk , fought for the bill to put sanctions on Russia in an attempt to pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine.

Darline Graham said she would have preferred to keep the sanctions in place because she did not trust Putin or Russia. She added that the legislation “meant a lot” to her late brother.

Trump ordered the sanctions pause on Russian energy just two days before they were set to take effect. The legislation passed both chambers of Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright also defended the waiver Sunday, arguing that it was meant to add pressure to end the war and was not an “economic lifeline” for Russia.

The halt drew criticism from several Republicans , including Sen. Thom Tillis (R- N.C.), who called it “beyond irresponsible.”

“It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Tillis wrote on social platform X.

Republicans have also spoken out against the president’s diesel deal with Moscow to import around 2.2 million tons of Russian diesel into the U.S. market.

articles.title: Democrats could win the Senate in 2026 but pay a price in 2028
articles.summary: These Democrats may be benefiting as much from Republican weakness and the national environment as from an affirmative embrace of their politics.
articles.body:
Every election matters, but the 2026 midterms may be among the most consequential in recent history.

Regardless of which party wins the House and Senate, the impact of next month’s elections will extend beyond November and into the 2028 presidential race. That is especially true in the Senate, where the parties’ closing arguments can make it sound as though senators serve only two-year terms, as Ramesh Ponnuru noted in the Washington Post.

Democratic candidates promise to check President Trump during his final two years and pursue investigations. Republicans warn that Democratic control would mean obstruction and efforts to “harass and impeach” Trump, Ponnuru noted. Either scenario could unfold, depending on who wins. But a narrow focus on the next two years misses the larger stakes.

Both parties enter 2028 at a crossroads. Republicans will no longer have Trump atop the ticket. Democrats still lack a clear identity or standard-bearer. The results will indicate where each party is headed.

For Republicans, the near-term direction is largely set. Trump remains in command, and whoever wins his endorsement will have the inside track to the nomination and an opportunity to reshape the party. Republicans still face a difficult post-Trump transition, but much of it may be decided for them.

For Democrats, the picture is far less settled. If they capture the Senate, four potential new senators who could provide the decisive votes — State Rep. James Talarico of Texas, Lieutenant Gov. Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, Troy Jackson of Maine and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan — would carry significant influence in 2028 and beyond.

The possibility of Democrats taking the Senate through those four candidates, along with former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in North Carolina, is hardly far-fetched. Trump’s approval rating is historically low, Democrats maintain an 8-point advantage on the generic congressional ballot and frustration with the economy continues to grow.

Yet a majority built through this group could encourage Democrats to conclude that the party’s progressive wing — not its moderates — offers the clearest path forward. That interpretation could leave the party vulnerable in 2028, as two features of this year’s contests suggest.

First, despite a strongly Democratic national environment, all four races remain close — even in relatively blue states, reflecting at least some voter unease with the candidates’ more progressive positions.

In Maine, Jackson holds an average polling lead of roughly 1 point over Republican Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), with some polls showing Collins ahead. Since winning the nomination after Graham Platner’s campaign imploded, Jackson has struggled to generate the same enthusiasm Platner inspired.

In Minnesota, Flanagan leads Republican Michele Tafoya by an average of just 2.6 points . That is striking, given Tafoya’s lack of political experience and Minnesota’s two-decade streak without a Republican senator.

In Texas, Talarico leads scandal-plagued Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by just over 2 points , despite Paxton’s vulnerabilities. Talarico is a gifted communicator, but Republicans have attacked his past positions on policing and transgender issues.

In Michigan, El-Sayed matches Flanagan for the top average lead of the four — still under 3 points. He has faced sustained criticism over past statements and struggled with Black voters in a primary he won by only 1 point.

In other words, these Democrats may be benefiting as much from Republican weakness and the national environment as from an affirmative embrace of their politics.

The second concern is that a majority built this way could leave Democrats politically beholden to an emboldened left. Already, a plurality of Democrats (44 percent) say they are voting to oppose Trump, rather than to support individual candidates’ positions or qualities, according to Politico . A Senate majority powered by anti-Trump sentiment may therefore prove difficult to sustain once Trump is no longer on the ballot or in the White House.

If a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028 with control of the Senate, progressives could pressure the party to pursue measures such as eliminating the filibuster, expanding the Supreme Court or sharply curtailing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

But the public is not necessarily there. Fox News polling found that 55 percent of voters view the Democratic Socialists of America unfavorably, and proposals associated with left-wing progressives remain potent Republican attack lines. Democrats therefore risk overreading a 2026 victory and moving ahead of the voters who delivered it.

It is also easy to imagine a replay of 2024, in which the party’s 2028 nominee is forced to answer for controversial positions taken by lawmakers whose victories helped create the majority. If Talarico, Flanagan, El-Sayed and Jackson hold the balance of power in the next Senate, Democrats may win the 2026 battle while complicating the 2028 war.

The lesson should not be that Democrats must reject these candidates. It is that an anti-Trump wave would not, by itself, amount to an endorsement of the party’s leftmost agenda, and the risks extend far beyond the end of Trump’s term.

For a Democratic Party still searching for an identity, confusing the two could push it decisively left just as the anti-Trump backlash begins to fade — and leave voters wondering what, exactly, they voted for.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die. ”

articles.title: Wicker calls on Trump, Zelensky to broker deal to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure
articles.summary: Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) is calling on President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to reach a deal to suspend Kyiv’s strikes on Russian petroleum facilities, which Trump has blamed for high domestic gas prices. Trump earlier this month unilaterally declared a ceasefire on striking important energy targets in Russia and…
articles.body:
Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) is calling on President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to reach a deal to suspend Kyiv’s strikes on Russian petroleum facilities, which Trump has blamed for high domestic gas prices.

Trump earlier this month unilaterally declared a ceasefire on striking important energy targets in Russia and Ukraine but Moscow repeatedly violated Trump’s declared moratorium, according to Zelensky.

Ukraine retaliated over the weekend by launching a massive drone attack on Moscow and St. Petersburg, and struck an oil terminal in St. Petersburg.

Now Wicker says Zelensky is ready to stop hitting Russian energy infrastructure and he urged Trump to negotiate a deal with him, despite recent tensions between the two leaders.

Wicker in a statement laid out what he called the “facts” underlying a possible deal:

“Fact 1: President Trump wants Ukraine to stop attacking Russian petroleum infrastructure,” he said.

“Fact 2: President Zelenskyy wants access to U.S. targeting assistance to stop Russian missiles from being launched at Ukrainian civilians from inside Russia.

“Fact 3: President Zelenskyy has agreed not to hit Russian petroleum in exchange for this targeting assistance.

“Fact 4: President Trump can lower prices at the pump today by simply agreeing to this deal!” he added.

Wicker, one of Ukraine’s most outspoken advocates in the Senate, urged Trump to accept the offer.

Wicker met with Zelensky recently on an overseas trip.

Relations between Trump and Zelensky hit a low point in recent days, as both leaders have criticized each other.

Zelensky criticized Trump for striking a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import millions of tons of diesel into the United States, despite Trump having signed into law last month a sanctions package targeting Moscow.

The Ukrainian leader said he felt betrayed by the Russia diesel deal and asked how Trump could be friends with Putin.

Trump on Sunday blasted Zelensky for hitting Russian oil facilities while knowing it would hurt American farmers, ranchers and businesses.

“Zelenskyy is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

“Farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this, but Russia is, nevertheless, sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World. Zelenskyy doesn’t care,” the president added.

articles.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle’s resignation doesn’t end an investigation — it changes the rules
articles.summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle’s departure as U.S. ambassador to Greece raises a question that often gets lost in the political headlines: What happens to a government investigation when the official at its center leaves office? The answer depends on who is conducting the investigation. Inspectors general, congressional committees and the executive branch operate under different legal authorities,…
articles.body:
Kimberly Guilfoyle’s departure as U.S. ambassador to Greece raises a question that often gets lost in the political headlines: What happens to a government investigation when the official at its center leaves office?

The answer depends on who is conducting the investigation.

Inspectors general, congressional committees and the executive branch operate under different legal authorities, and an official’s resignation affects each differently. Understanding how each institution operates is essential to evaluating what comes next.

President Trump’s decision to seek Guilfoyle’s resignation followed reports alleging improper financial dealings and other misconduct, allegations Guilfoyle has emphatically denied. Meanwhile, the State Department’s Office of Inspector General has reportedly been examining complaints involving her conduct , although the precise status and scope of that inquiry have not been publicly confirmed. And on Capitol Hill, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the ranking member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has made clear that his inquiry will continue despite her departure.

Taken together, these developments invite a familiar Washington temptation: treating a resignation as either confirmation of wrongdoing or an attempt to escape accountability . Neither conclusion necessarily follows. In reality, Trump’s decision, an inspector general inquiry and congressional oversight serve different purposes, operate under different rules, and can produce very different outcomes.

Consider first the White House’s decision. Ambassadors serve at the pleasure of the president, who retains broad authority to determine who represents the U.S. abroad. Trump did not need to wait for a formal finding of misconduct before deciding that Guilfoyle should leave her post. Such a decision can reflect concerns about diplomatic effectiveness, public confidence or the administration’s broader interests without resolving the underlying allegations.

While removing an official may resolve an immediate personnel concern, it does not necessarily resolve the questions that prompted scrutiny in the first place. This is where inspectors general enter the picture.

Unlike the president, whose decision may be focused on who should continue serving in a particular role, an inspector general examines the conduct and operations of the agency itself. Under the Inspector General Act , that responsibility includes investigating potential misconduct, identifying institutional failures, and recommending corrective action.

An official’s resignation does not automatically extinguish that authority. Inspectors general possess significant investigative tools by law, including access to agency records and authority to subpoena certain documentary evidence. Even after an official departs, questions may remain about whether agency safeguards were followed, how decisions were made, and whether institutional reforms are warranted.

Of course, the existence of an investigation is not proof of wrongdoing. Inspector general inquiries are fact-finding processes, not verdicts, and their conclusions must rest on evidence rather than allegations or political pressure. That caution is especially warranted when the underlying allegations are disputed.

Congressional oversight presents another layer of complexity — and perhaps the most misunderstood one.

Congress has broad authority to investigate matters relevant to its legislative responsibilities, including executive branch operations and government ethics. That authority can extend to former officials, particularly when their conduct bears on whether existing laws and oversight mechanisms are adequate. Yet Congress’s ability to seek information should not be confused with an unlimited power to compel it.

Garcia’s Oct. 14 letter, for example, reiterates requests for records and communications notwithstanding Guilfoyle’s resignation. While the request reflects a continuing interest by the committee’s Democratic minority, it is not itself a congressional subpoena. Under the House Oversight Committee’s rules , authority to issue subpoenas rests with the committee chair, subject to applicable House rules.

The distinction is more than a technicality. A voluntary congressional request and a duly authorized subpoena carry different legal consequences. The latter invokes compulsory process and potential enforcement mechanisms, while the former generally depends on voluntary cooperation. Understanding that difference is essential to evaluating both the authority of congressional investigators and the obligations of those receiving their requests.

With the November midterm elections approaching, however, that distinction could take on greater significance. Should Democrats gain control of the House, they could assume leadership of the Oversight Committee when the new Congress convenes in January, potentially transforming today’s voluntary inquiries into investigations backed by subpoena authority. Any such action would still require compliance with the rules governing the new Congress, and existing requests would not automatically become compulsory.

These institutional boundaries become even more consequential when multiple inquiries concern the same underlying conduct. An inspector general may seek to determine whether agency policies were followed. Congress may examine whether legislative reforms are necessary. Prosecutors, if warranted, may separately assess potential criminal violations. None of these inquiries necessarily dictates the outcome of another.

The danger is that political narratives can blur the boundaries between these processes. In Washington, a congressional letter can quickly become an “investigation,” an allegation can be treated as a finding, and a resignation can be portrayed as a confession. The legal process, however, demands greater precision.

The Guilfoyle situation illustrates why that precision matters. President Trump has exercised his authority to seek a change in diplomatic leadership. Whether other institutions have additional questions to pursue depends on their respective mandates, the available evidence and the legal tools at their disposal.

Accountability and fairness are not competing principles. Meaningful oversight requires both the ability to investigate potential wrongdoing and respect for the procedural safeguards that govern those investigations.

Resignation may close one chapter of public service. Whether it closes the investigation is an entirely different question, and one that must ultimately be answered by law, not political headlines.

Nadin Linthorst is senior counsel at Lex Politica PLLC, where her practice focuses on congressional oversight and investigations, government ethics and complex litigation. She previously served as assistant general counsel and acting unit chief at the Federal Bureau of Investigation, where she handled sensitive litigation and congressional oversight matters.
