articles.title: LEE CARTER: 2026 election could all come down to just one type of voter
articles.summary: Trump won voters who skipped 2020 and 2022 by 14 points, suggesting voter turnout could matter far more than party persuasion in the 2026 midterms.
articles.body: For decades, political consultants have been hunting the elusive swing voter. You know her. She's sitting in a Pennsylvania diner, staring into her coffee, agonizing over whether to vote Republican or Democrat. Pollsters call her. Reporters interview her. Campaigns spend millions trying to win her over. But maybe we've been looking for the wrong person. LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN What if the most important swing voter in America isn't deciding between Republicans and Democrats? What if they're deciding between voting and staying home? As a pollster, I've spent my career studying why Americans change their minds. But the numbers suggest we should be paying a lot more attention to Americans changing their habits. EVERYONE IS WATCHING TEXAS AND MICHIGAN. AS A POLLSTER, I KNOW WHERE THE REAL STORY IS Consider 2024. According to Pew Research, 12% of voters had skipped both the 2020 presidential election and the 2022 midterms, despite being eligible to vote. THE HISPANIC VOTE IS UP FOR GRABS IN 2026. CANDIDATES WHO IGNORE IT WILL LOSE President Donald Trump won that group by 14 points. Meanwhile, the people who voted in all three elections split almost evenly: Trump 50%, Harris 48%. And of all Americans eligible to vote in those three elections, just 41% actually voted in all three. We're spending fortunes trying to convince people to switch parties while millions can't be counted on to show up in the first place. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOUSE CONTROL COULD HINGE ON WHETHER THE OLD POLITICAL RULES STILL APPLY In 2022, Republicans won the House popular vote. But among people who voted in both 2020 and 2022, just 6% switched parties or voted for a third-party candidate in either election. As a pollster, I've spent my career studying why Americans change their minds. But the numbers suggest we should be paying a lot more attention to Americans changing their habits. What changed? Turnout. MIDTERM HISTORY MASSIVELY FAVORS DEMOCRATS. BUT THEY ARE MAKING A BIG MISTAKE Seventy-one percent of Trump's 2020 voters returned in 2022. Only 67% of President Joe Biden's did. Republicans didn't need millions of Democrats to change their minds. They benefited because more of their own voters showed up. Now consider the strange arithmetic of 2026. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Republicans have made enormous gains in voter registration since 2018. Their registration margin relative to Democrats has improved by eight percentage points in North Carolina, seven in Pennsylvania, five in Nevada and four in Arizona. These aren't polls. They're actual voter-registration records. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT But Democrats have something Republicans currently lack: greater reported enthusiasm. A new Pew survey finds 63% of Democratic House candidate supporters say they're extremely motivated to vote. Among Republican supporters, just 46% say the same. So, Republicans have strengthened their registration position. Democrats sound much more eager to vote. And neither party should be celebrating just yet. In 2022, America had its highest midterm voter-registration rate in decades. Yet fewer eligible Americans actually voted than in 2018. Apparently, filling out the paperwork is easier than finding your way to the polling place. Which is why, with less than three weeks until Election Day, I'd be paying less attention to another two-point movement in the polls and more attention to who's actually voting. Are the people who skipped the last midterms coming back? Are the voters Trump brought out in 2024 showing up without his name on the ballot? Will Democrats' enthusiasm translate into votes? And are those newly registered Republicans actually voting? Republicans have made enormous gains in voter registration since 2018. Their registration margin relative to Democrats has improved by eight percentage points in North Carolina, seven in Pennsylvania, five in Nevada and four in Arizona. These are questions neither party can afford to ignore. Of course, persuasion still matters. People change their minds. I've made a career studying how and why. But we've spent decades treating elections like a tug-of-war, with Republicans and Democrats fighting over a handful of voters standing in the middle. Sometimes the outcome changes because people switch sides. Sometimes it changes because one side shows up and the other doesn't. The swing voter hasn't disappeared. We've just been defining the swing too narrowly. The old swing voter was deciding who deserved their vote. The new swing voter doesn't necessarily switch sides. Sometimes, they switch off. articles.title: Trump approval hits record low in new survey
articles.summary: President Trump’s approval rating hit a record low in a new survey, with just over two weeks until voters decide which party will control Congress next year. The Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, released Sunday, shows Trump sitting at 33 percent approval. The rating is 4 points lower than a previous poll conducted in July, 8…
articles.body:
President Trump’s approval rating hit a record low in a new survey, with just over two weeks until voters decide which party will control Congress next year.

The Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, released Sunday , shows Trump sitting at 33 percent approval. The rating is 4 points lower than a previous poll conducted in July, 8 points lower than at this point last year and lower than at any other time during his first term.

Roughly 66 percent of respondents said they disapprove of his job performance, including 52 percent who say they strongly disapprove, according to the survey.

Democrats also received more support nationally from likely voters than their Republican counterparts, with 52 percent to 44 percent, respectively. Among registered voters, 50 percent backed Democrats over 42 percent that chose the GOP, the data shows.

Another 56 percent of respondents who said they are uncertain about voting next month or chose to vote early said they backed Democrats. Roughly 43 percent said the same about Republicans, according to the poll.

Just over 50 percent of respondents who voted in 2022 and 2024 say they lean toward Democrats compared to 47 percent of voters leaning toward GOP candidates.

As affordability concerns rise, 48 percent of voters said they are financially worse off than when Trump returned to the White House. This is the highest percentage seen by the polling partners since 1986.

Three-quarters of respondents collectively said the economy is “not so good” or “poor,” 1 point higher than was polled in 2022 and a near reversal from 2018, during the last midterm cycle under Trump, when 65 percent said the economy was “excellent” or “good.”

The dissatisfaction with the president’s job approval extends to the Republican Party, with 40 percent of registered voters saying they trust Democrats more with the economy than the GOP, at 33 percent.

But both parties remain highly unfavorable among U.S. adults, with 54 percent disliking the Democratic Party and 63 percent saying they are unhappy with the Republican Party. The GOP is also viewed as too extreme by 55 percent of respondents, while 36 percent say the same about Democrats.

Trump has called on voters to “ pretend I’m on the ballot ,” promising $5,000 to every U.S. adult if the GOP maintains control of both chambers of Congress. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday said the administration “ will own this economy ” and touted its successes through economic policy.

Consistent polling has shown that Americans remain largely concerned about the cost of living and the surging gas prices tied to the Iran war, which has been largely unpopular since it began on Feb. 28.

The Post-ABC-Ipsos survey was conducted Oct. 9-13 and included 2,545 respondents. The margin of error is 2 percentage points.

articles.title: Matthew McConaughey: ‘Independents belong’ in political fight
articles.summary: Matthew McConaughey is sharing a pre-midterm elections message, saying that voting for independent candidates could bring lawmakers “back to the middle, where most American values live.” In a video posted on X on Sunday, the “Interstellar” star said, “This is about the upcoming ballot, and I am not here today to endorse a candidate or…
articles.body:
Matthew McConaughey is sharing a pre-midterm elections message, saying that voting for independent candidates could bring lawmakers “back to the middle, where most American values live.”

In a video posted on X on Sunday, the “Interstellar” star said, “This is about the upcoming ballot, and I am not here today to endorse a candidate or a party. I am here endorsing two things: fairness and reality.”

“I believe in a fair fight, and a fair fight is not just two fighters throwing the same punches at each other for 50 years. A fair fight is when the fighters who ought to be represented in the fight are actually in the fight,” McConaughey said.

“The number one political identity in America today is not Republican. It is not Democrat. It is independent,” McConaughey said.

A 2025 Gallup poll found that 45 percent of U.S. adults identified as independents, compared to 27 percent each of respondents identifying as Democrats or Republicans.

“So independents belong in the fight — not as a protest, not as a spoiler — but as a real and potential winner, on the ballot and considered seriously by us,” McConaughey said.

“Our birth certificate is not the Declaration of Compromise — it is the Declaration of Independence. And a true independent is not a fence sitter, Mr. or Mrs. In-Between,” McConaughey, who’s flirted with a political bid himself over the years, told his more than 2.8 X followers.

“A true independent is not even against the R’s or the D’s. A true independent takes the best of both, and that’s not indecision,” he said.

Touting former Sen. Joe Manchin’s (I-W.Va.) organization, the Independent Leadership Council, which the ex-lawmaker launched earlier this year aimed at recruiting and electing independent candidates, McCounaghey said, “Joe Manchin knows the math — lived it in a 50-50 Senate. One independent mind became the deciding vote and took all the fire for it alone.”

“Now imagine that same power held by three or four together, owned by no party at all,” he said.

The political system, according to the 56-year-old performer, “has never been more lopsided.”

“In 2024, 87 percent of U.S. House seats were effectively decided in party primaries by just 7 percent of eligible voters,” McConaughey said.

“For most Americans, the real election is over before they ever even show up in November. And that’s not competition — that’s more like a scrimmage, one team playing against itself, deciding the season for everybody else.”

“Understand if the goal is to change how both parties behave. If the goal is to bring them back to the middle, where most American values live, then electing independents is a mechanism to make that happen,” McConaughey said.

“The reality is, midterms are coming, and this November, in more places than ever, you do have more than two choices,” the Academy Award winner said.

“I’m not telling you who to vote for. I’m telling you to look at your ballot and study up. See if they represent you, what you believe in,” he said.

“Check if they can be that voice of reason, and if they can, treat them like a potential winner because they can be,” McConaughey said.

“That’s what fairness looks like. That’s what reality allows for the first time in a long, long time.”
